Imprisonment in a prison and corrective labor camp in Tashkent, Uzbek SSR, is the first item in declassified CIA document 0000102958, dated November 2, 1986. The heading spells the city Tashket. A second item follows in the title, but its subject is cut off.

The summary says suspects waited in investigative prisons before trial, while most convicted inmates went to labor camps. Camps were grouped as general, reinforced, and severe, based on security and inmate privilege. Notorious or important convicts could stay in prison, where guards kept a closer watch. The text also notes Uzbek inmates usually kept to themselves.
cia-0000108158: Current Situation and Probable Developments in Finland During 1954 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108158, dated January 3, 1964. The catalog date and the heading disagree by ten years: the file is dated 1964, the title says 1954. That mismatch stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is a Finland outlook item with a dating puzzle.
cia-0000109058: The Che Guevara Diary is the short subject of declassified CIA document 0000109058, dated November 5, 1967. The heading names a diary tied to Che Guevara, in four plain words. No place or campaign is named in the title itself. The brief record is a diary item, filed a month after Guevara's death in Bolivia in October 1967.
cia-0000119758: An October 1956 CIA chronology lists the principal events of the Hungarian Revolution from October 23 to November 4. Timelines assembled while events still moved became the first draft of the uprising's history, and this one lays the revolution out day by day. A day-by-day list gave officials a shared spine of fact during arguments about response, and it still serves readers as the uprising's basic timetable.
cia-0000126958: A July 1968 CIA special memorandum examines the split in the AD party and what it meant for Venezuelan democracy. Accion Democratica, the country's leading party, was breaking apart from within. The memo weighs how that feud threatened the party system holding the country together. Party splits in a dominant-party system move the whole state, and the memo's concern was that Venezuela's young democracy might crack along with its strongest party.
cia-0000132158: Dated January 1991, Iraq-Kuwait situation report 475 covers a deleted section and first political reactions to an event the heading loses mid-phrase. Whatever drew the reactions was removed by the censors. The report preserves the rest of that day's watch. Deleted passages are marked rather than hidden in these releases, so readers can see the shape of the missing piece even where its words are gone.
cia-0000132758: Venezuela's stance on the Cuban problem fills a CIA paper dated May 1, 1960. Caracas was still making up its mind at that stage of the quarrel. The stance would harden into open hostility within about two years. For now the paper catches a government mid-decision. The short paper sets out the views held in Caracas that spring.
cia-0000135858: A declassified CIA cable dated 6 February 1952 turns to a proposed meeting with Castillo, raised years before he led the force that invaded Guatemala. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136258: 6 May 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA situation report about daily operations situation report number 5, the daily count rising in the final weeks. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136858: Was a man a government plant? This cable to LINCOLN asks the station to check. A trusted source calls him a ringleader of the Salama uprising. The uprising failed on 28-29 March 1953. Papers said four leaders were shot escaping jail. Three others found asylum in the Mexican embassy. The source suspects a setup. The ringleaders may have been government agents in a fake uprising. They now enjoy a paid vacation in Mexico, he says. Verify before any request goes on.
cia-0000141158:
Word reached the CIA in November 1961 that B-26 number 933, painted with Cuban markings, lay deep in jungle a few miles from the Bocay River in Nicaragua. The wreck held the remains of two men. General Somoza's forces were heading to the crash site by helicopter to inspect it, and word came back asking what should be done with the remains and the men's effects.

Headquarters replied that 933 had left Boca Chica on 16 April for the base called Tide and never arrived. A small team was to fly to Managua, reach the site, and gather charts, maps, notebooks, and other gear, once local approval came through.
un-ga-res-2758:
On 25 October 1971 the UN General Assembly voted to seat the People's Republic of China in place of the Republic of China. Resolution 2758 says the Beijing government's team are the only lawful voice of China at the UN. It also confirms China as one of the five permanent members of the Security Council, with veto power.

The vote shut the door on the team of Chiang Kai-shek, which had held China's seat since 1945 from its base on Taiwan. From that day, Beijing took China's place in the Assembly, the Council, and all linked UN bodies. Few single votes have changed the UN more.
un-ga-res-a-69-58:
A rare high-level meeting on nuclear disarmament, held on 26 September 2013, is followed up in Resolution A/69/58, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Strong support at that meeting for swift, real steps toward the total end of nuclear arms is stressed. The text voices deep concern at the ruinous toll any use of such arms would take on mankind.

The Assembly calls for fast heed of the legal duties states owe on disarmament. Wide support for a full pact on nuclear weapons is backed. Talks should start at once in the Conference on Disarmament on such a pact, one that bars the arms in all forms and provides for their destruction. A world meeting on the point is set for no later than 2018.
un-sc-res-258: Year 1968 in the catalog holds Resolution 258, a formal Security Council decision of the United Nations. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-458: Acting formally, the Security Council produced the decision numbered 458, catalogued under 1979. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1358: For the year 2006, the catalog lists Resolution 1358 among the Security Council's formal decisions. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1658: Under the number 1658, the Security Council's formal decision is held in record wording transcribed by Wikisource. The members' method is visible on the page: establish the situation, invoke earlier action, then decide. For readers tracing UN practice, that method matters as much as any single outcome, and the full text shows both.
un-sc-res-1858: In 2009 the Security Council adopted Resolution 1858, and this collection keeps the official text through a Wikisource transcription. The act's preamble aligns fifteen governments on one description of a situation; its operative part aligns them on one response. Preserving both alignments, word for word, is the service performed by this entry.
cia-0000135658: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 1 January 1961 and flags that date as estimated. Brigade 2506 was the CIA's exile army, then training for the Bay of Pigs landing. A New Year's Day date on an estimated record suggests paperwork logged at the start of the year rather than a known event. No subject is recorded for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, one of many similar records from the brigade's final winter.
plos-pone-0000058:
Yuan-Ping Pang pointed drug designers at a fresh target for stopping malaria mosquitoes in a 2006 paper. Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme in the insect nervous system, and poisons that block it are a main class of insecticides. Resistance and harm to other species limit the old compounds, which hit a well-known site on the enzyme.

Pang identified a novel target site on acetylcholinesterase, a fresh place where a control agent might bind. A new site raises the hope of insecticides that kill malaria-carrying mosquitoes while sparing humans and helpful insects, and that work even where resistance has beaten the old sprays. For a disease spread only by these mosquitoes, better control tools save lives directly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d58: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 26, 1943, as the Moscow Conference neared its close. His message is Document 58 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. October 26 was a crowded day in the volume, full of letters between capitals and conference rooms. The record for this one gives the date and the names and nothing narrower. It survives in the Foreign Relations series with the rest of that day's traffic.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d158: An editorial note dated May 5, 1943 stands as Document 158 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, far from the volume's opening where its twin note sits. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series mark seams where the editors joined bodies of papers, and this one opens the Moscow Conference section that follows. Reading it tells the reader whose files the next papers came from and how the editors handled them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d258:
The Chinese record of a Cairo conversation between President Roosevelt and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek is introduced by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. No official American record of the talk was found, and none appears to have been prepared, so the editors print a Chinese summary instead.

The Chinese government held the record in its own files, had it translated from Chinese, and gave leave for its printing in 1957. The note also flags gaps in the Log. The Log lists the Chiangs, Hopkins, and Colonel Elliott Roosevelt as dinner guests. The colonel's own account gives no sign he attended. Topics his book adds, missing from the Chinese summary, include a coalition government for China, British rights in Shanghai and Canton, and the future of Malaya, Burma, and India.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d358:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the first meeting between President Roosevelt and Marshal Stalin, at Tehran on 28 November 1943 at three in the afternoon. The two leaders had never met, and Roosevelt opens with pleasure: he has tried for a long time to bring this about.

Stalin blames the delay on military business. Then he gives a frank front report. The Soviets have lost Zhitomir and are about to lose Korosten. They hold the initiative elsewhere, but can attack only in the Ukraine. Roosevelt says he wishes he could pull thirty or forty German divisions off the Eastern front, a question he wants Tehran to address. Talk turns to postwar trade and a surplus merchant fleet for Russia. It turns then to China, whose fighting Stalin faults on its leaders. Last comes Lebanon, which Roosevelt blames wholly on de Gaulle's committee.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d458: Number 458 in the Cairo-Tehran volume is an editorial note. Department historians use the note form to speak in their own voice. They add facts, explain references, and point to other documents. The record here covers the Allied conferences of late 1943. Strategy for Europe and Asia dominated those meetings. So did early arguments about the postwar world. The note gives readers footing before the papers resume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d558:
A second Churchill message to President Roosevelt is dated March 4, 1944, hard on the heels of the first. The pair continues the dense exchange of that week. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Two messages a day, two days running, tells its own story about March 1944: the invasion was three months off, and every theater's claims collided in the leaders' in-trays. Churchill separated his subjects into single papers, and Roosevelt answered in kind. For readers, this message helps reconstruct a week of alliance management at full stretch, preserved because the State Department printed the conference volumes generously.
frus-1944-quebec-d58:
President Roosevelt answered Prime Minister Churchill on September 6, 1944. The reply appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, among the final pre-conference exchanges.

Roosevelt's answers that week kept the welcome warm and the American positions intact. He faced a guest who would argue hard for Britain's share in the Pacific war and for generous aid terms, and the President's letters prepared his ground. For readers, this message closes the transatlantic preparation: within a week the two men would be talking across a table in Quebec City instead of across an ocean.
frus-1944-quebec-d158:
Admiral Leahy wrote to Hull for the Joint Chiefs on August 29, 1944, giving the military view of French participation in the war against Japan. Indochina, the letter stresses, lies in the China theater and is an area of American strategic responsibility. It quotes the views Chiang Kai-shek expressed at Sextant on how the two theaters should divide Thailand and Indochina.

From a military standpoint, the chiefs concurred with the British proposals. One exception mattered: French participation in planning political warfare should be restricted to the Southeast Asia Command area. The letter also counsels recognizing French desires about Indochina where consistent with American policy, with extent and timing kept under continuing review.
frus-1944-quebec-d258:
Control of the strategic bomber forces in Europe is addressed in C.C.S. 520/4, the United States Chiefs' paper of September 13, 1944. With Allied armies now on the continent, the wartime arrangement under Eisenhower's direction was ending. The Americans agreed in principle with joint control by the RAF's Deputy Chief of the Air Staff and the commander of the United States Strategic Air Forces in Europe.

Those two officers, Bottomley and Spaatz, would act jointly for Portal and Arnold as agents of the Combined Chiefs. The Americans found the British draft directive inadequate in several respects, however, and attached a revised directive of their own. The Combined Chiefs approved it, as amended, the following day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d58:
From Moscow on 16 January 1945, Ambassador Averell Harriman reported to President Roosevelt on where the American party would sleep at Yalta. His top secret telegram is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It deals with rooms, not strategy.

Harriman says Roosevelt will stay in the Livadia palace, the czar's former summer home. The site has one building of 21 rooms, one of 41, and a third once used by guards. Space for the enlarged military party is still unsure, so he is asking the Soviets for more rooms. The support ship Catoctin, he notes, can only be based at Sevastopol.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d158:
Stalin answered Roosevelt on Poland on 29 December 1944, and the answer closed the door. His message, received in Washington in translation, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. He had the President's note of the middle of the month in hand.

On the American statement of 18 December, Stalin says he would rather speak in person; in any case, events in Poland have moved well past it. Intercepted radio traffic, he charges, proves that talks with Mikolajczyk screened men who waged criminal terror against Soviet officers and soldiers in Poland. arxiv-2606-00058: Quantum computing changes the security landscape — for better and worse. This survey covers security with quantum computing. The survey maps threats and defenses in the quantum era. Quantum computing threats are coming eventually. Serious preparation starts with deep understanding.
arxiv-2606-07458: Arrays of atom-like emitters packed below a wavelength emit collectively — even with inhomogeneous broadening. This paper studies that collective emission. The findings matter for quantum light sources. Quantum light sources rely on collective emission. Inhomogeneous broadening threatens the coherence.
arxiv-2606-07658: Brain surgery shifts the brain — neurosurgeons need synthetic intra-operative MRI from ultrasound to compensate. This paper provides it. The synthesis guides the scalpel.  Neurosurgery requires precise real-time guidance. Synthetic MRI from ultrasound compensates for brain shift during operations. Surgeons operate more safely.
tob-4058:
The first volume of Isis Unveiled, from 1877, takes on the science of its day. Its subtitle claims a master key to the riddles of old and new science and faith. H. P. Blavatsky argues that a science of mere matter can not explain magnetism, trance cures, or the feats of the seance room. Old wisdom, she says, can.

Fierce, stuffed with quotes, and prone to wander, the book runs from the magic of Egypt to the lab tests of her own age. Some claims fall flat now, but the attack still bites. As the first shot of the Theosophic cause, the volume made its author famed at once.
tob-4158:
William James delivered the Gifford Lectures published in 1902 as The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature. Under its full title, the classic approaches religion through the people who live it. Converts, mystics, and saints describe their experiences in their own words, quoted at generous length, and James asks what those states are worth.

Healthy-minded believers, sick souls, divided selves, and sudden conversions each receive a hearing before his pragmatic test: judge by fruits, not roots. The lectures founded the psychology of religion as a field. Philosophy here listens to life before theorizing about it, which is why the book still recruits readers across every belief and none.
tob-4161-70458:
Edward B. Tylor, often called the father of anthropology, published Primitive Culture in 1871. Volume one argues that culture develops in stages, much as living things were then said to evolve. Tylor studies tools, customs, language, and myths as evidence of that growth.

He treats myth as early man's honest attempt at science, an effort to explain dreams, death, and disease. Old customs that linger as mere habits, he calls survivals, and he tracks them like fossils. The book gave the young field its program and its name for its subject. Victorian readers met here a bold claim: all peoples share one mental history.
tob-0158:
Seventeen hymns stand at the oldest layer of the Avesta: the Gathas, sung in an archaic tongue and credited to Zoroaster himself. Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie translated them for English readers. No other part of the Zoroastrian scriptures carries the same weight, since the prophet's own voice is heard here.

The hymns praise Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord, and urge hearers to choose good thoughts, good words, and good deeds against the Lie. Their monotheism is stark and early, from the dawn of recorded religious history. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, Guthrie's version lets the three-thousand-year-old songs speak plainly.
aelian-works-hercher-1858:
Claudius Aelianus, a Roman-era Greek with a storyteller's ear, left two great stores of lore. Aelian's works, in Rudolf Hercher's 1858 edition, gather all that survives of him in one set. Seventeen books On the Nature of Animals stand first in the file.

Beside them sit the Historical Miscellany, a heap of short tales and facts, plus his letters and fragments. Bees, elephants, kings, and fools pass through his pages in bright, brief scenes. Naturalists mined him for animal lore; tale tellers mined him for plots. Hercher's edition is the full Aelian in one scholarly home.
heuvelmans-on-track-of-unknown-animals-1:
Bernard Heuvelmans, a Belgian zoologist, gave the hunt for unknown beasts its first full map in 1958. On the Track of Unknown Animals, in Richard Garnett's English rendering, is the founding book of cryptozoology. Seven parts and nineteen chapters sweep the globe for hidden life.

Heuvelmans weighs reports of the orang-pendek, the yeti, sea serpents, and a mammoth said to live in the far north woods. He sorts strong tales from weak ones and asks what beast each could be. His method treats rumor as a clue to be tested, not a joke. The book shaped every beast hunt that came after.
cardano-metoposcopia-1658:
Girolamo Cardano reads fate in the brow in Metoposcopia, his vast Latin work of 1658, set in print at Paris. Cardano was a healer, sage of sums, and gambler of famed note. He holds that the lines of the brow are writ by the stars at birth. Each line, cross, and scar marks health, wealth, rank, and the hour and kind of a man's death in his scheme.

Eight score draws of brows fill the book, each with its gloss. The scheme is false, yet its craft stuns. The text is the brow lore's great store. Sages still cite its plates.
hansard-admission-of-baron-de-rothschild:
The House of Commons record for July 26, 1858 tells of the day Baron Lionel de Rothschild took his seat at last. Hansard, the verbatim record of Parliament, holds the whole scene in its pages. He had been chosen by the City of London for eleven years, yet kept out by the form of the oath.

The law was changed so a Jew could swear on the Old Testament and sit in the House. Lionel, the head of the London house, thus became the first professing Jew to sit in the Commons. The record is the high point of the long fight for Jewish rights in Britain.
swedenborg-heaven-and-hell-1758:
Emanuel Swedenborg, a Swedish sage and man of science, wrote this account of heaven and hell in Latin in 1758. The text here is the English form in which most readers have met it. Swedenborg had once been a lead mind of his land in mines, maths, and the work of the body.

He tells of the worlds of spirits he said he saw and roamed for years in trance. Heaven, hell, and the mid realm each have their lands, towns, and laws in his calm scheme. The book founds the faith that bears his name and marks the lore of the West.
swedenborg-earths-universe-1758:
Emanuel Swedenborg said spirits from other worlds spoke with him at length. His Earths in the Universe came out in 1758. He tells of trips in spirit to the Moon and to the planets. Each world holds folk with its own traits and faith.

Swedenborg tells how the folk of Mars, Venus, and the rest live and pray. He links their traits to parts of the mind and body. Later occult readers drew hard on these strange tales. The book is the oddest claim of many worlds from its age. His tales still draw readers who chase the roots of the other-worlds idea.
swedenborg-heaven-hell-1758:
Emanuel Swedenborg wrote Heaven and Hell in Latin in 1758. He said he had spent years in talk with angels and spirits. The book gives his full map of the worlds past death. It is his most read work and the base text of his church.

Heaven, hell, and a mid world of spirits each get a full tale. Swedenborg says the dead keep a form, a home, and work much like life here. None are sent to bliss or pain by a judge; each drifts to his own kind. The book shaped views of the next life for two hundred years.
herodotus-histories-rawlinson-1858:
Herodotus wrote his Histories in Greek in the fifth century BC, and George Rawlinson gave England its standard version in 1858 to 1860. Rawlinson, an Oxford scholar, added maps and learned notes. His brother Henry, famed for cuneiform work, helped with eastern lore.

Herodotus tells how Greece fought Persia and won against huge odds. Along the way he reports Egypt's customs, Scythian rites, and marvels galore. He mixes inquiry, travel tales, and speeches into one wide survey. Later ages named him the father of history, with cause. His notes draw on fresh finds from Egypt and Persia.
starkey-pyrotechny-asserted-1658:
George Starkey was an American-born chymist, raised in Bermuda and trained at Harvard, who worked in London's alchemical circles. His Pyrotechny Asserted and Illustrated, published in 1658, defends alchemical practice against its scorners. Starkey taught the writer known as Philalethes, whose books spread his methods worldwide.

Pyrotechny, the art of fire, is Starkey's name for the furnace work by which metals and medicines are made and tested. He answers critics with experiments, weights, and furnaces rather than with riddles alone. The book shows the most skilled American-born chymist of the seventeenth century arguing for his craft in public.
linnaeus-systema-naturae-vol1-1758:
Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae appears here in Volume 1 of its tenth edition, dated 1758. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands in Latin. The tenth edition is the starting point of zoological naming, the baseline every later name is checked against.

Volume 1 covers Animalia, the animal kingdom, arranged in classes from mammals to worms and insects. Linnaeus gave each species a two-part name, genus and species, the binomial system science still uses. He placed humans among the primates, a bold step for his age. The volume founded binomial nomenclature for animals and remains the reference from which zoology counts its naming history.
morris-defence-guenevere-1858:
William Morris was twenty-four when The Defence of Guenevere appeared in 1858. It was his first book and the first volume of Pre-Raphaelite poetry published in England. Morris, a wealthy young Oxford graduate, filled it with the medieval world he loved.

In the title poem, Queen Guenevere defends herself before Arthur's court against charges of betrayal, arguing with passion and cunning. Other poems retell Arthurian tales and dark medieval stories of love and violence. The verse is vivid, strange, and deliberately old-fashioned in diction. The book sold poorly at first but now stands as a landmark of Victorian medievalism.
longfellow-miles-standish-1858:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published The Courtship of Miles Standish in 1858, drawing on the history of Plymouth Colony written by his own ancestor. Longfellow claimed descent from John Alden himself. The poem sold tens of thousands of copies within weeks, in America and England alike.

Captain Miles Standish, the colony's blunt little military leader, loves the newcomer Priscilla Mullins but is too awkward to court her. He sends his young friend John Alden to plead his case. Priscilla's answer became famous: why don't you speak for yourself, John? The love triangle plays out against Indian alarms, sickness, and the work of planting a colony. Longfellow's hexameters helped make Plymouth the American origin story.
holmes-autocrat-1858:
Oliver Wendell Holmes published The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table in 1858, gathering essays he had run in The Atlantic Monthly. Holmes, a Harvard doctor and professor, imagines himself as the autocrat of a Boston boarding-house table. His monologues, interrupted by fellow lodgers, made him famous on two continents.

The Autocrat discourses on everything: conversation, poetry, trees, theology, and the young fellow who sits across the table. Poems break up the talk, including The Deacon's Masterpiece, about a carriage built so logically it ran a hundred years. Holmes's wit is learned, warm, and quick with metaphor. The book founded the American familiar essay's reigning style and stayed a favorite for generations.
marguerite-de-valois-memoirs-1658:
Marguerite de Valois, queen of Navarre and wife of Henri IV, wrote her Mémoires around 1594 about the court she grew up in. They were first published in 1628, and the English translation of 1658 carries them here. Marguerite was sister to three French kings and daughter of Catherine de Medici, placed at the heart of power and danger.

Her memoir covers the French wars of religion from inside the palace, with weddings, plots, and the shadow of massacre. She writes with grace and self-defense, eager to set her own story straight. The book became the classic insider memoir of the Valois court. Its voice, a queen's own, still sounds clear across four centuries.
comte-catechism-1858:
Auguste Comte recast his positivist system as a catechism in 1852, and Richard Congreve Englished it in 1858. Positivism, Comte's philosophy, trusted science as the guide for modern society. Late in life he shaped it into a Religion of Humanity. The catechism form sets the teaching out as questions and answers.

A priest of the new faith instructs a woman who asks what positivism requires. Their talk covers worship, morals, family, and the order of society. Humanity itself, not God, stands as the object of devotion. The book shows Comte's system in its most personal form. It puzzled some followers and bound others closer.
nightingale-subsidiary-notes-nursing-185:
Before her famous nursing work took shape, Florence Nightingale wrote her Subsidiary Notes in 1858. The memorandum, privately printed, treats female nursing in military hospitals in peace and war. She drew on her Crimean War experience with sick and wounded soldiers. The paper laid out how army nursing should be organized and trained.

Her plan covered staffing, discipline, pay, and the standing of nurses in the ranks. It became the policy paper behind the Nightingale Fund. That fund built the training school that reshaped nursing. The Gutenberg text preserves a reform at the planning stage. Readers see her mind working on systems, not slogans. It rewards close study.
liddell-scott-abridged-greek-lexicon-185:
Henry Liddell and Robert Scott published their great Greek-English Lexicon in 1843, and the abridged version, nicknamed the Little Liddell, followed for students. The 1858 printing comes from the sixth edition of the parent work. Generations of schoolboys and undergraduates learned Greek with it open.

The abridgment keeps every common word with its main senses, forms, and constructions, in compact type. Students could carry it where the giant lexicon could not go. Liddell, dean of Christ Church, was also the father of Alice, of Wonderland fame. This little book remains a monument of Victorian classical schooling.
allibone-critical-dictionary-english-lit:
Samuel Allibone, a Philadelphia bookseller and bibliographer, published Volume One of his Critical Dictionary of English Literature in 1858. It covers authors from A to J. The full work notices some 30,000 British and American writers.

Each entry gives the author's life, a list of works, and judgments gathered from reviews and histories. Forty subject indexes help readers find writers by theme, from poetry to voyages. Allibone labored for years among his own vast book collection. The dictionary became the great Victorian bio-bibliography, the first place to learn what an author wrote and what critics said of it.
plos-pone-0003458:
Rita A. Busuttil and co-authors measured mutation buildup without a DNA repair protein in 2008. Ku80 helps join broken DNA ends, a quick repair route called non-homologous end joining. Losing that route has been tied to early aging. The team used mice missing Ku80 for their tests.

They counted mutations at a reporter gene, LacZ, across tissues and cells. Both the rate and the kinds of mutations changed without Ku80. The data show which errors pile up when end joining fails. That helps link broken repair to aging and cancer risk.
plos-pone-0003558:
Elena Lesma and co-authors tested a targeted antibody against tumor cells in this 2008 paper. Tuberous sclerosis complex causes benign tumors called hamartomas across organs. Faults in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes drive the syndrome. The team grew smooth muscle cells lacking TSC2 from a patient's tumor.

An antibody against EGFR, a growth factor receptor, was applied to those cells. It inhibited their proliferation efficiently and specifically. Blocking that receptor may offer a treatment path for this syndrome. A related lung disease, LAM, might benefit from the same approach. Tumors in this syndrome are benign yet can still harm by their size and place.
plos-pone-0003658:
Irini Evnouchidou, Frank Momburg, Athanasios Papakyriakou, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The immune system displays protein pieces on cell surfaces so T cells can inspect them. An enzyme called ERAP1 trims those pieces down to the right size first.

The team found that the inner sequence of a piece, not just its ends, decides how ERAP1 trims it. That finding changes how the final displayed set is predicted. Knowing the trimming rules helps explain which pieces reach the surface and thus what the immune system gets to see.
plos-pone-0003758:
Xiaodian Sun, Li Jin, and Momiao Xiong published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. The dynamics of a system decide how cells, tissues, and organisms behave. Building math models of biochemical networks means estimating their hidden parameters from data. That estimation is the hard part.

The authors adapt the extended Kalman filter, a classic engineering tool, to nonlinear state-space models of such networks. The filter infers parameter values as measurements come in. It helps turn noisy observations of living chemistry into working models of metabolism and gene regulation.
plos-pone-0003858:
Min Pi, Ling Chen, Min-Zhao Huang, and colleagues published this mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2008. GPRC6A is an orphan receptor found across the body. In lab dishes it senses amino acids, osteocalcin, and calcium-like ions. What it does in a living animal was unknown.

The team created mice lacking GPRC6A and characterized their condition. The null mice showed osteopenia, feminization, and metabolic syndrome together. The triple phenotype reveals one receptor quietly governing bone strength, sex traits, and metabolism at the same time. One missing part thus touched bone, sex traits, and body fuel use.
plos-pone-0003958:
Julia Szendroedi, Elisabeth Zwettler, Albrecht Ingo Schmid, and co-authors measured muscle energy output after acromegaly in 2008. Faulty mitochondria and fat stored in muscle link to poor insulin action. Acromegaly, an excess of growth hormone, also reduces insulin sensitivity. The team asked whether effects linger after the disease is treated.

Their PLOS ONE article studied patients with previous acromegaly. Basal ATP production in their skeletal muscle ran low. That lasting deficit may help explain ongoing metabolic risk. The result argues for long follow-up of metabolism after hormone excess ends. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004058:
Darren J. Gray, Gail M. Williams, Yuesheng Li, and co-authors modeled a parasitic disease in China in 2008. Schistosoma japonicum infects over one million people in China. Another forty million live where infection risk is present. Unlike its relatives, this species also infects many animals.

Their PLOS ONE article studies transmission in lake and marshland regions. Animal hosts keep the parasite cycling even when people are treated. Models that include animals fit the disease's persistence better. Control programs must target the whole transmission web, not humans alone. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004158:
Jérôme Rollin and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. ID2 is a regulator that helps control the balance between cell growth and cell specialisation. In healthy cells it keeps that balance; recent work has tied it to cancer.

The team examined where ID2 sits inside cells in non-small cell lung cancer, whether in the nucleus or outside it. They report that this intracellular location carries predictive value for the disease. In other words, the same protein sends a different message depending on its address inside the cell. A marker like that could help doctors judge how a patient's cancer is likely to behave.
plos-pone-0004258:
Tara Smith and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2009. MRSA, the drug-resistant form of Staphylococcus aureus, had been found in many pigs and pig farmers in the Netherlands and Canada. No study had checked carriage among swine and swine workers in the United States.

The team swabbed the noses of 299 swine and their handlers in the Midwest. They report that the MRSA strain ST398 is present in both the animals and the workers. The finding raised a new occupational and food-chain question for American public health. Swine workers, in other words, can carry what their pigs carry.
plos-pone-0004358:
Natalia Gottig and colleagues published this plant pathogen study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. citri causes citrus canker, a damaging disease of citrus crops. The bacterium has several protein secretion systems. They include at least one type V system of the two-partner secretion pathway, mainly used for moving large proteins out of the cell.

The team studied a filamentous hemagglutinin-like protein handled by that system. They report that it is involved in the bacterium's virulence. A surface protein that helps the pathogen attack citrus is a possible target for protecting groves.
plos-pone-0004458:
A small sea creature that can regrow its whole brain offers a fresh model for nerve repair, present Carl Dahlberg, Helene Auger, Sam Dupont, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The creature is the tunicate Ciona intestinalis, a marine animal related, distantly, to backboned animals. Unlike us, it can regenerate nerves and a complete adult central nervous system.

Good new models of regrowth are in short supply, and each must come with tools for lab work. The team refined this model, setting out the resources and methods that make it practical. A creature that rebuilds its brain on cue lets scientists watch repair step by step. What it does naturally may suggest what might be coaxed, one day, in injured human nerves.
plos-pone-0004558:
An antibody test can show a tumor dying in response to chemotherapy, report Fares Al-Ejeh, Jocelyn Darby, Chris Tsopelas, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer therapy aims to kill malignant cells. Directly measuring tumor cell death in the body would be a valuable part of monitoring whether a treatment is working.

The team had developed an antibody, called APOMAB, that binds a target named La, exposed on dying cells. Here they show it detects the apoptotic tumor response to life-prolonging, DNA-damaging chemotherapy. In plain terms, a scan could reveal whether a tumor is dying weeks before it shrinks. Knowing early whether a drug works lets doctors switch failing treatments sooner and spare patients useless side effects.
plos-pone-0004658:
The structure and working mechanism of an enzyme that can both cut and build sugar chains are solved by Jie Yin, Lei Li, Neil Shaw, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzymes are endo-beta-N-acetylglucosaminidases, shortened to ENGases. They are dual specificity enzymes, able to catalyze hydrolysis, breaking down, and transglycosylation, building up, reactions.

Because of that two-way talent, ENGases have become a focus of intense research for the synthesis of glycopeptides, molecules part protein and part sugar. The team determined the structural basis and catalytic mechanism for one member, Endo-A. Knowing exactly how the enzyme grips and cuts its substrate lets chemists retune it. Better glycopeptide synthesis matters for making uniform antibody drugs and vaccines.
plos-pone-0004758:
Angela Lai, Murray Cairns, and Nham Tran built a random small RNA library to find RNAs that shift complex traits in mammal cells. In PLOS ONE in 2009. RNA based silencing has given strong tools to find and test genes. Small RNAs can turn down single genes with high precision in cultured cells and in animals.

The team built a library of random small RNAs that cells can produce. Screening that library can reveal RNAs that change cell behavior in desired ways. Such screens may find new drug leads and gene roles. They work without knowing the target in advance.
gadbury-doctrine-nativities-1658:
John Gadbury teaches birth-chart astrology in Genethlialogia, his Doctrine of Nativities, from 1658. The great English manual tells how to cast a horoscope and read a life in it. Gadbury, rival to the famed Lilly, served the Civil War generation with forecasts drawn from the stars at each client's birth.

Rules for houses, aspects, and judgments fill his orderly, confident pages. Health, wealth, marriage, and death all submit to his method here. Judicial astrology stands at its most systematic in this work. Readers meet the heavens treated as a book of lives, open to any reader who learns the signs aright.
harris-treaty-1858:
Townsend Harris, the first American consul in Japan, negotiated the 1858 treaty of amity and commerce with the Tokugawa shogunate. Four years after Perry's visit, the United States wanted real trade, not just ports for supplies. Harris argued that Japan could gain from open commerce, even as British and French power loomed over Asia.

The terms opened more ports to American ships and let Americans live and trade in set districts of Japanese cities. They also fixed low tariff rates and gave foreigners legal protections outside Japanese courts. Many Japanese saw the deal as unequal and humiliating, and anger at such terms helped fuel the movement that later toppled the shogunate.
french-constitution-1958:
France adopted the constitution of the Fifth Republic in 1958, presented here in its first, unamended form. The Fourth Republic had collapsed under the strain of the Algerian war, and Charles de Gaulle returned to power on his own terms. Michel Debré drafted the charter under de Gaulle's direction, meaning to cure the ills of shifting parliamentary rule.

The text builds a strong presidency: the president names the prime minister, can dissolve the assembly, and holds wide powers in an emergency. Parliament keeps the laws, but within limits the charter sets. Voters approved the text by a large margin in a referendum. The law that tamed the chaos of the Fourth Republic still rules France today, amended since but unmistakable in its design.
cia-0000009758:
Bodies believed to be those of twelve American prisoners of war were found in the Viet Cong's Duy Xuyen district, a January 1973 report states. Duy Xuyen lies in Quang Nam province, on South Vietnam's central coast. The discovery came as the Paris accords were being signed.

A find of this size could close a dozen cases at once, if identification held. Officials had to test the claim carefully before telling any family. The report's careful wording, possibly twelve, shows that caution at work. It preserves a grim discovery at the exact moment the war was supposed to end.
cia-0000009858:
An assertion about many captured American pilots, its ending cut off in the heading, fills an April 1966 item with two deleted sections. The deletions hide the claimants, as the censor's marks show. What survives is the claim's shape: many pilots, captured, and something asserted about them.

Files like this one frustrate readers, yet they still testify. A claim large enough to file in 1966 mattered to the men tracking prisoners then. The redactions mark where the public record stops, not where the story does. Preserved as released, the item shows both wartime reporting and later secrecy at work.
cia-0000011758:
Che Guevara had vanished from public life in Cuba. In August 1966 the CIA issued a statement on his status and on Havana's timetable for spreading revolution. Guevara, the Argentine doctor turned guerrilla, had helped Castro win power and then disappeared from view. Rumors placed him fighting in Africa or preparing a new campaign in Latin America.

The statement reports what the agency believed about where Che was and what he meant to do. It also lays out Cuba's plans for exporting revolution to other lands. Within a year Guevara was dead in Bolivia, which makes the paper a record of the hunt.
cia-0000013858: A senior American pilot, a lieutenant colonel, was captured in Thanh Hoa Province, and a CIA note dated June 4, 1967, records it. Senior rank made a capture stand out in the files. A high ranking prisoner held strong value for the north, both for news value and for what he knew. The note marks his entry into the prison system.
cia-0000014658: Headquarters wished to pass on material about a convicted spy's case, in a CIA file dated April 1, 1956. The title keeps the spy unnamed in the open line. Passing case material between offices was the daily flow of the spy files. Even a cover note like this shows how long the big cases stayed alive on paper.
cia-0000014758: The pro-Cominform Communist Party in Trieste is tracked in a CIA file dated January 5, 1953. The file leans on CIC reports, from the Army's counter intelligence arm. Trieste was a disputed port city, split between east and west claims. Party moves there mattered because the city's fate hung in the balance.
cia-0000015258: Bolivia's reports clashed on the details of a fallen object, in a CIA file dated April 3, 1978. Two days of claims had already muddied what came down and where. Clashing reports were the norm for falls in far country. The file preserves the muddle before any team could reach the site.
cia-0000015358: An item for the Director's log fills a CIA file dated March 2, 1953. The title does not say what the item was. The Director's log noted matters thought fit for the top man's eye. A saucer era item reaching that log shows how high the subject could rise in the building.
cia-0000015458: Comments and suggestions from the UFO panel fill an undated CIA item filed in 1953. The panel was a group of scientists asked to judge the saucer evidence for the government. Their added remarks show experts refining what should be done next. Even without a firm date in the catalog, the entry holds the tone of that first official review and its advice.
cia-0000026758: The outlook for Iraq is forecast in a CIA paper dated in 1957. Iraq was then a kingdom allied with Britain, ruled in the name of a young king. Within a year the monarchy was destroyed in a bloody coup. Read with that knowledge, a calm outlook paper from 1957 shows how fast the ground of the Middle East could shift under careful men.
cia-0000037158:
Caucasian prisoners were transferred by truck from Thanh Hoa to Quang Ninh province, a CIA record dated February 1, 1982 reports. Thanh Hoa lies south of Hanoi, and Quang Ninh far to the northeast. A truck convoy between them was a long and notable move.

The record preserves the reported transfer as a piece of prison-system movement. Tracking where prisoners were held, and when they were moved, helped test other claims. The file shows analysts building a picture of a hidden system from single glimpses. Each convoy report added a line to a map drawn mostly in the dark.
cia-0000040058:
Peru's Armed Forces Command issued a communique on a killing, in a CIA record dated March 2, 1987. A communique is the military's formal public statement on an event. Peru was then fighting the Shining Path insurgency across much of the country.

Inside, the command's own wording sets out the official account of the killing. Such statements were how the military spoke to the public during the war. The file preserves the official line at a set date. Readers can set it beside press and human rights accounts of the same years, and judge how the command chose to present its actions.
cia-0000045158:
The FMLN claimed credit for killing Marines, in a CIA record dated May 5, 1985. The claim concerned the Zona Rosa killings in San Salvador. Guerrilla claims of this kind were issued to be believed and feared.

Inside, the rebels' claim of responsibility is preserved as made. Owning the attack told Salvadorans the rebels could strike at will. It also dared Washington to answer in the war's daily contest. Claims like this one were answered, in time, with more aid and more advisers for the government. The file holds that boast from May 1985, set beside a companion communique record from the same attack in this same group of files.
cia-0000045258:
From Panama, Ungo denied any link with the negotiations, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. Distance was the point of his denial's dateline. An exile leader in Panama could not be running talks in San Salvador.

Inside, his clearing of his own name is preserved as issued. Denials from abroad carried a special need to be believed. His hosts, his allies, and his enemies all read this one closely. The file holds the Panama denial among the case's many disavowals. Each one drew the map of who would, and who would not, be tied to the crime.
cia-0000049058: The second part of the file on the legal case involving Hans Christ survives in a CIA item from 1983. The same item touches on the forming of a new Salvadoran group, its title cut off before naming it. Case files like this one advanced in pieces, each part adding a hearing, a ruling, or a delay.
cia-0000049258: The Latin America warning and forecast meeting of February 1990 is preserved in a CIA item from that year. Warning meetings were where analysts told their bosses what to watch: coups, offensives, and collapses they saw coming. The record shows the region as the watchers framed it, one month into a new decade.
cia-0000049358: El Salvador: Political Difficulties Persist heads declassified CIA document 0000049358, dated September 4, 1982. plos-pone-0004858:
Sonja Grosskinsky and colleagues found a multifunctional surface protein Borrelia recurrentis uses to escape innate immunity, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Borrelia recurrentis causes louse borne relapsing fever with severe disease and high mortality. It evolved strategies including antigenic variation to evade immune defense. The team identifies for the first time a surface protein combining anti complement, anti opsonic, and invasive functions.

One protein performs three escape jobs at once. Such efficiency suits a genome reduced pathogen. Targeting it could restore immune clearance. Relapsing fever remains neglected globally. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0005458:
Dik Heg and co-authors studied helper fish in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In some animal groups, young helpers stay with a breeding pair and help raise young that are not their own. One idea says helpers pay for their place on the home ground by working.

The team watched female cichlid helpers and checked which ones later bred themselves. Helpers that worked more were more likely to breed. That link fits the pay-to-stay idea, though other gains may matter too. The study adds real-world evidence to a long debate about why animals help raise others' young.
plos-pone-0005558:
Thomas Duda and Taehwan Lee studied venom change in a sea snail at Easter Island in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When a species escapes its old rivals and enemies, it may spread into new roles and change fast. Far less is known about the gene changes behind that release.

The snail Conus miliaris is a hunting cone snail whose venom kills its prey. At Easter Island it faced a new setting with fewer rivals. The team compared its venom genes there with those elsewhere to see how release reshaped its weapons. Venom genes change fast even in normal times, which makes the island shift stand out more clearly.
plos-pone-0005658:
Olive Li and co-authors combined flu polymerase parts from birds and mammals in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Flu viruses swap gene parts when two strains infect one animal, creating new strains. One part from bird flu had entered both human pandemic strains of the last century.

The team tested all mixes of the three polymerase parts from bird and mammal strains. Some mixes worked far better than others, which helps predict which swaps could yield a pandemic virus. That foresight supports flu surveillance worldwide. Surveillance teams use exactly such rankings when they judge which bird viruses to watch most closely.
plos-pone-0005758:
Ahmed Moustafa and co-authors traced the origin of toxin-making genes in cyanobacteria in 2009. Saxitoxin causes paralytic shellfish poisoning, a sometimes fatal illness from eating tainted shellfish. Marine algae make most of it, but cyanobacteria in fresh water carry the genes too.

Where those genes began, and how they jumped between groups, was little known. The team compared gene sequences across species to read that history. Knowing how toxin genes spread helps predict which blooms may turn toxic. It also feeds the broader story of how bacteria trade useful, or harmful, toolkits.
plos-pone-0005858:
Macy Heung and co-authors compared in 2009 two maternal blood fractions for spotting fetal messages during pregnancy. The placenta sheds its own messenger RNA into the mother's blood, raising hopes for noninvasive prenatal tests. Whole blood had seemed a promising source since placental RNA was found there.

The team found fetal-specific RNA is actually easier to detect in plasma than in whole blood. Cells in whole blood add noise that drowns the faint fetal signal. The practical lesson is simple: plasma is the better starting material. Getting the source right is step one for any blood-based prenatal test.
plos-pone-0006458:
Tarek Boussetta and co-authors tested a plant oil compound against gut inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, drive inflammation by releasing reactive oxygen species. A signal called TNF alpha primes them to release even more. Standard anti-inflammatory drugs do not always control this process well.

The compound, punicic acid, is a fatty acid found in pomegranate seed oil. The title reports that it blocks TNF-driven neutrophil overactivation. It also protects rats from experimental colon inflammation. A food-derived compound with this profile could interest doctors seeking gentler options. More work would be needed before any human use.
plos-pone-0006558:
Charlotte Ling, Leif Groop, Silvia Del Guerra, and colleagues measured a diabetes-linked protein in human pancreatic islets for PLOS ONE in 2009. Calpain-10 was the first gene identified influencing type 2 diabetes risk by positional cloning. Studies in beta-cell lines and rodent islets suggested roles for the protein. The team measured its expression in islets from patients with type 2 diabetes.

Their title reports that calpain-10 expression is elevated in those islets. Higher levels in real patient tissue strengthen the gene's link to disease. It also raises the question whether lowering it would help insulin secretion. The study grounds a famous diabetes gene in human data.
plos-pone-0009458:
Hanako Kobayashi and co-authors reported on a signal protein and sepsis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sepsis is a whole body crisis sparked by infection. Too much inflammation damages blood vessels and organs. The protein, interleukin-32 beta, occurs in human tissues. Normal lab mice do not have it, which had hidden its role.

When the team gave the protein to mice, vessel inflammation grew worse. Sepsis also became more severe in those animals. The result names the protein as a driver, not a bystander, in the crisis. Blocking it could be a new way to calm the immune storm that makes sepsis so deadly.
plos-pone-0009558:
Beatriz Martinez-Poveda and co-authors tested plant compounds against blood vessel growth in PLOS ONE in 2010. New vessels feed growing tumors, so blocking them is a cancer strategy. Hyperforin, from the herb St. John's wort, already showed strong blocking power. The team made and tested two new relatives of it. Their names are tetrahydrohyperforin and octahydrohyperforin.

Both new compounds proved to be potent blockers of vessel growth. Comparing them with the parent compound shows which chemical features do the work. That knowledge helps chemists design better versions. It is a step toward turning a plant product into a cancer drug lead.
plos-pone-0009658:
Andre Le Jeune and co-authors studied a bacterial defense in a gut germ in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enterococcus faecalis lives in the gut and can cause serious infections. It withstands lysozyme, an enzyme in tears and saliva that kills many bacteria. A factor called SigV helps run its stress defenses. The team tested SigV's role in the germ's original model strain.

SigV proved key both to lysozyme resistance and to the germ's virulence. Without it, the bacterium was easier to kill and less harmful. That makes the factor a point of weakness worth probing. Understanding how gut germs resist our enzymes helps explain how they turn dangerous.
plos-pone-0010458:
Caroline Aspord and colleagues built a cancer vaccine from a special donor cell type in PLOS ONE in 2010. Effective cancer vaccines remain elusive despite decades of effort. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are rare immune cells with strong anti-tumor potential. Their use in therapy had not been worked out. The team used donor cells matched to a common tissue type marker. Matching lets one donor line serve many patients.

An off-the-shelf vaccine would be far easier than growing each patient's own cells. The matched cells could present tumor pieces to the patient's immune system. This study tested whether that strategy can stir real anti-tumor responses. It points toward standardized cancer vaccines, if the responses prove strong and safe. Rare cells, here, might serve many patients.
plos-pone-0010558:
Joana Duarte and colleagues shifted immune cell balance to prevent autoimmune arthritis in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic disease where immunity attacks the joints. Two T cell types pull in opposite directions in this disease: Th17 cells drive attack, regulatory cells calm it. Their balance may decide whether arthritis starts. The team tested a non-depleting treatment that adjusts two key markers, IL-17 and Foxp3.

Adjusting the balance protected mice from developing the arthritis. Rebalancing rather than suppressing immunity wholesale is an attractive strategy. It promises fewer side effects than blanket immune shutdown. Mouse prevention does not equal human treatment, but the principle is clear. This study supports therapies that retune, rather than remove, immune cells.
plos-pone-0010658:
Eduardo Rodriguez-Noriega and colleagues built a scoring system for flu triage in Mexico, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic flooded hospitals with people who had breathing problems. Clinicians at one Guadalajara hospital needed a fast way to sort mild cases from dangerous ones.

Their score combined patient history, lab results, and chest images. Applied to adults with flu-like illness, it separated those needing admission from those safe to send home. A tested score beats guesswork when wards are full. The Guadalajara experience offers a template other hospitals can adapt in the next pandemic.
plos-pone-0010758:
László Bányai, Peter Sonderegger, and László Patthy found a new binding role for agrin, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Agrin is best known for organizing the junction where nerves meet muscle. Part of the protein had a clear job there. The rest of this large protein had stayed largely unexplained after two decades of study.

The team showed agrin can bind three growth factors from the BMP and TGF-beta families. Binding can store, shield, or present such factors to cells. That gives the unexplained parts of agrin plausible work in growth and repair. A famous specialist turns out to hold a second, more general job.
plos-pone-0010858:
Katherine Elliott, Eleftheria Zeggini, Mark McCarthy and co-authors published this large collaborative analysis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variants in the HNF1B gene are tied to type 2 diabetes, and oddly, the same variants seemed to lower prostate cancer risk. The team asked whether the effect reaches other cancers or belongs to prostate cancer alone.

Pooling data from nineteen genome-wide studies, they examined two common variants across tens of thousands of cancer cases and controls. The cancers included bowel, breast, lung, and pancreatic tumors, plus melanoma. Results differed sharply between datasets, driven by opposite effects in prostate cancer versus the other cancers. Elliott and colleagues conclude the HNF1B effect is not a general cancer shield. Their work is a caution against treating one gene's role as the same in every tissue.
plos-pone-0010958:
Estefanía Rodríguez and Marymegan Daly published this sea anemone evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Anemones live in every ocean habitat, including deep-sea vents and seeps where chemistry, not sunlight, fuels life. Species from those extreme sites are highly specialized and their classification is confused, so the authors rebuilt their family tree from DNA.

Using five molecular markers across the superfamily that holds most deep-sea, polar, and vent anemones, they tested whether the vent dwellers form one clan. They do not: anemones of chemical environments descend from at least two separate lineages, one mostly deep-sea and one mostly shallow-water in origin. Rodríguez and Daly show that extreme habitats were colonized more than once, reshaping how anemone diversity is organized.
plos-pone-0011058:
Renata Dziedzic, Manjot Kiran, Przemyslaw Plocinski and co-authors published this tuberculosis cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bacterial division begins when FtsZ protein assembles into a ring at midcell. How the TB bacterium controls that step was largely unknown. The authors focused on ClpX, part of a protein-degrading machine, whose production rises when the bacterium infects the immune cells called macrophages.

Four independent binding methods confirmed that ClpX physically interacts with FtsZ. Adding ClpX raised the amount FtsZ needs before it can form its ring. That restrains assembly. Cells normally keep the two proteins in a fairly tight ratio. Dziedzic and colleagues identify a brake on the division machinery of a pathogen that divides slowly and unevenly. Interfering with division control is a recognized route to new antibiotics.
plos-pone-0011158:
Pappas, Viswanathan, Chandrasekaran and colleagues revisited a past pandemic in PLOS ONE in 2010. Viruses of the H2N2 flu type caused the 1957 pandemic and later vanished from humans, though they still exist in animals. The team tested how well these viruses bind cells and spread.

Their work gauges whether this old flu type could pose a threat again. Most people alive now lack immunity to it, since it left human circulation long ago. Knowing its binding and spread traits helps planners judge risk. The study supports readiness for a forgotten virus that could return.
plos-pone-0011258:
Drogemuller, Becker, Kessler and colleagues studied greyhounds with nerve disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some greyhounds develop polyneuropathy, a weakening of nerves across the body. The team searched their DNA and found a deletion in a gene already linked to a similar human nerve disease.

The shared cause mirrors human Charcot Marie Tooth disease in a dog breed. That parallel helps both veterinary care and human medicine, since each species can teach about the other. Breeders can now test for the deletion to reduce affected puppies. Researchers gain a large animal model whose disease matches the human one closely.
plos-pone-0011358:
Yaye Lawaly and co-authors asked in 2010 whether some people are born more likely to pass malaria to mosquitoes. When a mosquito bites a person carrying malaria parasites, it can pick up the parasite and spread it onward. People differ greatly in how infectious they are, and that human pool of infection keeps the disease alive in a region.

The team tested whether that infectiousness runs in families, which would point to a heritable trait. Their evidence supports a genetic share in how strongly a person can infect mosquitoes. If a small share of people fuels much of the spread, control programs could focus on finding and treating those people. The finding shifts part of malaria control from the mosquito alone toward the human hosts who most feed transmission.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1258:
Prime Minister Suzuki of Japan spoke at a press conference on 28 July 1945. His words gave the world's first public sign of Tokyo's answer to the Potsdam Declaration, issued two days before. The statement reached Washington fast and was read there as a refusal.

Suzuki used a word, often rendered as killing the terms with silent contempt, that hardened Allied views. Whether he meant flat rejection or a wish to wait for Moscow, the effect was the same. The summit's leaders took Japan's answer as no. This statement is that answer in its public form, a hinge on which the war's last weeks turned.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1358:
George Allen wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn for a third time in this run on 25 July 1945. Allen's Near Eastern and African affairs office kept a steady file of papers flowing to Dunn during the conference. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Dunn sat close to the center of the American effort at Potsdam, so papers addressed to him reached a man who could act. The Allen notes show a regional bureau working its questions into the summit's crowded agenda. For readers tracing Middle East policy in 1945, the Allen papers are a thread worth following. It runs from start to end of the volume's closing section.
frus-1945-50-intel-d58:
Brownell, an executive officer for the assistant secretary of war for air, wrote to the Lovett Committee members on 17 December 1945. The committee's work was still live at year's end. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Staff officers keep committees alive: they call the meetings, circulate the drafts, and chase the members' views. Brownell's memorandum shows that machinery turning in December, weeks after the Lovett report. Readers might pass over such a paper, but it marks something real, the refusal of a hard question to die. The intelligence design was still being argued in committee rooms while the secretaries settled its outline above.
frus-1945-50-intel-d158: A memorandum dated 28 June 1946 was prepared for the Secretary of State's Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Langer). It is document 158 in the Foreign Relations volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Notes of this kind put a matter before one named man, so work could move at once. His office led the State Department's own research and intelligence work at the time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d258:
A memorandum from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Assistant Director for Special Operations (Galloway) on 22 December 1947. It is document 258 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d358:
Dated 1 January 1949, "Report From the Intelligence Survey Group to the National Security Council" comes from the top level of the government. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 358 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

Reports were the heavy guns of paper work: slower than a memo, but built to end an argument. The replies it drew, kept near it in the files, show how the findings stood up to attack. The report is the Dulles Report. It holds the survey team's full findings and its fixes for the young CIA, sent to the Council in early 1949.
frus-1861-d58:
On 1 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams at the London legation. The letter is document 58 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

July opened with Congress called to meet and the armies near Manassas. Seward's first of July letter keeps faith with the plan set in spring. It guided Adams through the weeks just before Bull Run, when a quick Union win still seemed within reach. Congress met on 4 July and voted men and money, which backed Seward's bold tone abroad. Men and money voted at home were the facts that gave his words abroad their weight.
frus-1861-d158:
On 21 October 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to William Dayton. It is document 158 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The paired form appears in the Paris file as in the London one. Each letter owns its point and its answer. Together they show how a single day's French business could fill two files and still leave the desk clear. Two files, two answers: the habit kept replies swift and the record clean. A clear desk at day's end was Seward's small, daily victory over the war.
frus-1861-d258:
News and judgment from James Shepherd Pike reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 9 October 1861. It was printed as Document 258 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the autumn of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d58:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 5 May 1862. It was printed as Document 58 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d158:
Document 158, dated 10 October 1862, carries a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It sits in the long Great Britain section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Three days earlier, William Gladstone had said in a speech at Newcastle that the South had made a nation. Words Union men read as a push toward British backing for the Confederacy. Adams had to answer that mood in London. Seward's steady mail, of which this letter is part, armed him with Washington's position week after week. Seward trusted Adams's calm judgment and rarely overruled the man on the spot.
frus-1862-d258:
William L. Dayton reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 18 March 1862, in a letter printed as Document 258 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton represented the United States in Paris as its minister.

Mid-March brought the Union's Peninsula campaign toward Richmond just as France was deciding to go it alone in Mexico after its allies pulled back. Dayton reported on a court balancing two American ventures at once. His letters are a chief source for how Napoleon III's government weighed the Confederate cause against its Mexican design that spring. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d358:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, addressed Henri Mercier on 20 February 1862 in a letter printed as Document 358 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It closed a run of three Seward letters to the French minister in two weeks.

Late February 1862 was a bright moment for the Union, with Fort Donelson fallen and Nashville about to follow. Seward negotiated from strength that month, a fact foreign legations registered. His letters to Mercier in this window show a secretary using good news as diplomatic capital while it lasted. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d458:
On 22 June 1862 John Lothrop Motley sent this report from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 458 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Motley wrote as McClellan stood before Richmond and Europe waited to see if the Confederate capital would fall. Austria, busy with its own Italian and German problems, kept a strict and chilly neutrality. His report told Washington how the war's climax looked from the Danube. Letters like this one, from a minor post in the great question, still mattered. Seward's map of Europe had to be complete. Vienna's silence was itself a fact worth recording.
frus-1862-d558:
On 18 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels. The instruction is Document 558 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote the day after Antietam, in the same mid-September round that reached Madrid, Vienna, and The Hague. Sanford's Brussels post gave him a window on French and British thinking through King Leopold's wide family web. Orders to such a post mixed the government's line with requests for what the minister was hearing. The dispatch shows Seward gathering Europe's reaction to the autumn crisis through his most connected small-post minister, even before the battle's result was fully known.
frus-1862-d658:
William H. Seward addressed this letter to Robert H. Pruyn on 19 December 1861. Pruyn was the incoming American minister to Japan, named to follow Townsend Harris. The letter appears as document 658 in the Foreign Relations volume printed for 1862.

In the last weeks of 1861 Seward sent Pruyn a run of letters, each adding to the charge the new envoy would carry. They dealt with the work of the legation and the stance the United States meant to keep in Japan. This one is a mid-run piece, useful chiefly as part of the full set that sent Pruyn off with his orders in hand.
frus-1863p1-d58:
Secretary of State William H. Seward resumed the London file with this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 19 January 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 58 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, set after the Confederate papers.

The volume's order puts the foe's captured letters between two runs of the London mail, and this letter picks the thread back up. Seward wrote to keep Adams aimed at the standing aims: no British aid for the South, no warships out of British yards. It is a hinge piece, joining the winter run to what came before.
frus-1863p1-d158:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 April 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 158 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day late in April shows the ship question still filling the post's plate. Adams gave the yards, the talks, and the press each a sheet. This one opens the set of 17 April. In the volume's long London run, the day is one more crest in a spring of crests. Each charts Britain's slow turn from the South's hopes.
frus-1863p1-d258: On 25 July 1863, a Mr. Hyland wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 258 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the papers on relations with Britain during the Civil War. The record gives no first name or office for the writer, so the letter stands simply as one citizen-era note in the wartime mail.
frus-1863p1-d358:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 10 January 1863. It stands as document 358 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d458:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington directed a letter to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 11 April 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d558:
In the flow of wartime mail, William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 8 June 1863. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d658:
The 9 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?
