The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020158:
Jun Wu, Thomas J. Klein, and Marek Mlodzik studied signal receptors in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. Frizzled receptors pass Wnt signals, which guide growth and body pattern. The authors tracked where in the cell these receptors sit, a trait set by their inner tails.

Where a receptor sits decides which signals it can send. The team's work shows the tail acts like an address label, sending the receptor to the right cell compartment. That placement then tunes the strength and kind of signal that follows. The study adds a layer to how Wnt signaling is controlled, a pathway that is central to development and often goes wrong in cancer.
plos-pbio-0020258:
Jennifer L. Nemhauser, Todd C. Mockler, and Joanne Chory studied plant hormone cross-talk in PLOS Biology in 2004. Plants use hormones called brassinosteroids and auxin to guide growth. Both affect stems, roots, and leaves, so their signals must be coordinated rather than sent in isolation.

Using the model plant Arabidopsis, the team showed the two pathways lean on each other. Many genes respond to both signals, and blocking one changes the effect of the other. That interdependence is a design rule for plant growth control. It matters for farming, since tweaks to one hormone path will ripple into the other. The paper helped move plant science past single-hormone thinking.
plos-pone-0000158:
Paul D. Waters, Gauthier Dobigny, Peter J. Waddell, and colleagues published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. LINE-1 is a jumping gene, a stretch of DNA that copies itself into new spots in the genome. It makes up a large share of mammal DNA. The authors trace its history across the major clades of placental mammals.

By comparing LINE-1 across species, the team reconstructs when this element was active and how it spread. The story helps explain why mammal genomes differ so much in size and content. It also gives a backdrop for the many gene changes that jumping elements cause, for better and worse.
plos-pone-0000258:
Michael J. Angilletta, Robbie S. Wilson, Amanda C. Niehaus, and colleagues published this urban ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, under the heading of urban physiology. It reports that city ants possess high heat tolerance, handling temperatures that would trouble their rural kin. Cities run warmer than the countryside, a heat island effect ants must cope with.

Urban animals are evolving under new pressures, and heat is one of the sharpest. The authors compare the heat tolerance of city ants with what the species normally shows. The result is an early data point in the study of how wildlife adapts to city life.
plos-pone-0000358:
Justin D. Blethrow, Chao Tang, Changhui Deng, and colleagues published this proteomics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents a modular mass spectrometric tool for analyzing protein complexes. The tool reads what the complexes are made of, and how their parts are phosphorylated, chemically tagged in ways that switch activity. The tool's modules can be combined as needed.

Protein complexes run the cell, and their tags change with conditions. A modular instrument workflow makes such analysis more routine and flexible. The paper is a methods contribution to proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins, as it moved from listing parts to mapping their states.
plos-pone-0000458:
Jennifer Hartt Meyers and colleagues studied how HIV weakens a specialized immune cell, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are the body's champion producers of interferon, an alarm signal against viruses. The team measured the impact of HIV on these cells' survival and on their antiviral activity.

If HIV kills or disables the very cells meant to raise the alarm, the immune system starts the fight already handicapped. Documenting that damage helps explain why HIV infection so often becomes chronic. It also points to protecting or restoring these cells as a possible treatment strategy, alongside drugs that attack the virus directly.
plos-pone-0000558:
Yuri B. Yurov and colleagues examined chromosome errors in the developing human brain, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Aneuploidy means a cell carries the wrong number of chromosomes; confined chromosomal mosaicism means only some cells in the tissue are affected. The team documented both in brain development.

The brain was long assumed to be chromosomally uniform. Finding mosaicism there raises questions about how much variation is normal and whether abnormal patches contribute to disease. Counting chromosomes cell by cell in developing tissue is slow work, but it set reference points for later claims about the mosaic brain.
plos-pone-0000658:
Andrei I. Ivanov, Moshe Bachar, Brian A. Babbin and colleagues singled out one motor protein at the seams between surface cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Epithelial sheets form barriers, and their strength depends on the apical junctional complex, built from tight and adherens junctions. Actin filaments beneath the surface regulate that complex. Myosin II, a major actin motor, was already implicated.

The team reports a unique role for one form, nonmuscle myosin heavy chain IIA, in regulating these apical junctions. Unique means the other forms do not simply cover for it. Barrier breakdown drives gut and skin diseases, so knowing which motor holds the seams matters.
plos-pone-0000758:
Christophe Fraser developed simpler ways to estimate how fast a new epidemic is spreading, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Reproduction numbers, the average number of people infected by a typical case, play a central role in tracking outbreaks. His aim was methods simple enough to be applied as an epidemic emerges, when data are thin and decisions cannot wait.

Fraser separates individual and household reproduction numbers. Spread within households behaves differently from spread between them, and mixing the two distorts forecasts. Estimating both gives a clearer picture of whether an outbreak will take off. Methods papers like this become the toolbox reached for in the first weeks of a crisis.
plos-pone-0000858:
Li-Tzu Chen, Tzu-Ping Ko, Yu-Wei Chang and colleagues probed five charged building blocks in an archaeal DNA repair protein, for PLOS ONE in 2007. RecA family proteins run an ATP-dependent DNA strand exchange, in which a single-stranded DNA filament finds and pairs with a matching double-stranded sequence. Despite more than 20 years of effort, the molecular mechanism of homology pairing and strand exchange was still not fully known.

Their RadA protein comes from archaea, microbes with ancient molecular machinery. The five conserved positively charged residues sit in the L1 and N-terminal DNA-binding motifs. Structural and functional analyses of exactly those residues test how the protein grips DNA during the search for a match.
plos-pone-0000958:
Alexander Statnikov, Chun Li and Constantin Aliferis studied how environment, genes and analysis choices can mislead a cancer gene hunt, in PLOS ONE in 2007. New genotyping tools let researchers scan the whole genome for variants tied to disease. Early studies suggested panels of markers could flag esophageal cancer risk.

The authors warn that pitfalls in data analysis, and tangled effects of environment and genetics, can inflate such claims. Their paper is a caution worked through a real case. Gene wide studies are powerful, but only when the statistics respect how messy human data are. The work is aimed at everyone building risk panels.
plos-pone-0001058:
Naohiro Kawamura, Fumitaka Kugimiya, Yasushi Oshima and colleagues studied a signaling protein's role on both sides of bone turnover, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bone mass is held by balance: osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts resorb it, under many local and body wide controls. Akt is one of the key serine threonine kinases in that control web.

The team examined Akt1 in both cell types. A single protein acting in builder and demolisher alike could coordinate the two, keeping turnover matched. Bone diseases from osteoporosis to arthritis involve that match failing. Knowing which Akt form sits where helps target treatment without upsetting the other side.
plos-pone-0001158:
The prion protein is famous for its role in transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, diseases such as scrapie and BSE. Yet its normal job in the body is still unclear. Marius Lötscher and colleagues found an unexpected one in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using histology, immunochemistry, and PCR-based methods in mice, they linked the protein to immune defense.

The team reports that induced prion protein controls retroviruses that the immune system activates in the mouse spleen. In other words, when the spleen's defenses switch on, prion protein helps keep resident retroviruses in check. That gives the protein a concrete normal function to set beside its disease role.
plos-pone-0001258:
Long QT syndrome is an inherited heart rhythm disorder that can kill without warning. John Bankston and colleagues report the case of a newborn carrying a new mutation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The mutation sits in SCN5A, the gene for the heart's main sodium channel, and caused the variant called LQT-3.

The authors describe the de novo mutation as novel and lethal, with distinct molecular pharmacology and a distinct therapeutic response. De novo means it appeared fresh in the child, not inherited. Working out how this channel variant answers to drugs guided treatment of a very young patient.
plos-pone-0001358:
Arcobacter butzleri is a bacterium found in human clinical cases, a member of the epsilon subdivision of the Proteobacteria. William Miller and colleagues present its complete genome sequence in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. It is a close relative of established pathogens such as Campylobacter jejuni and Helicobacter pylori.

The authors worked out the full genome sequence of the human clinical isolate. A complete sequence shows what the bacterium can do, and which of its genes might help it cause disease. For a little-studied relative of two major pathogens, the genome is the reference everything else builds on.
plos-pone-0001458:
Frank Schweitzer and Robert Mach published a 2008 PLOS ONE paper on the spread of giving. When a cause takes off, gifts can surge like an outbreak. The pair show that a disease spread model fits this surge well. In their frame, word of a cause passes from person to person like a germ.

Herding plays a key role, as donors watch what the crowd does through the media. The model uses a shared field that stands for that media pull over time. A good fit lets groups forecast how a drive will rise and fade. It also hints at when a push will do the most good.
plos-pone-0001558:
Michiel van Boven and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on when people will take flu drugs. Drugs that curb viruses hold promise for new ills such as bird flu and SARS. But the drugs are not free of harm, so people weigh gain against risk. The team modeled when self interest and group gain pull in unlike ways.

In their model, what pays for one person can fail the group as a whole. That gap can stall a drug drive that needs wide uptake to work. Plans must thus align the two, with clear rules and fair access. The work frames a social snag that pure drug science cannot solve.
plos-pone-0001658:
Juliette Salvaing, Anja C. Nagel, Emmanuèle Mouchel-Vielh, and their co-authors studied two gene-control proteins in the fruit fly in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Polycomb group proteins keep genes switched off over the long term, while trithorax group proteins keep them on. Together they hold gene patterns steady through development, above all for Hox genes, which set body layout.

The paper centers on Corto, a protein that works with both camps, and its interaction with Cyclin G. The full text gives the binding tests, the fly genetics, and where the two proteins meet. Their meeting point links the on-off memory system to a protein better known from cell growth. It may explain how Corto fine-tunes gene patterns as the fly develops.
plos-pone-0001758:
Nuo Yang, Jia Huang, Joel Greshock, and their co-authors studied how an ovarian cancer gene is switched on in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. PIK3CA is boosted, amplified, or mutated in ovarian and other cancers, making it a promising drug target. How it gets over-activated in living tumors was unclear.

The team reports that NF-κB, a master inflammation switch, transcriptionally regulates PIK3CA in the ovarian cancer microenvironment, the tissue setting around the tumor. The full text gives the gene activity tests and the binding evidence. If inflammation switches on a growth gene, then anti-inflammatory strategies or NF-κB blockers could complement drugs aimed at PIK3CA itself.
plos-pone-0001858:
Robin M. D. Beck, Henk Godthelp, Vera Weisbecker, and their co-authors described the oldest marsupial fossils of Australia in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. New skull and body fossils come from the early Eocene Tingamarra Local Fauna. The team refers them to Djarthia murgonensis, known before only from broken tooth remains.

The new finds show Djarthia is a member of a distinct marsupial group. Its kinship bears on how marsupials reached Australia and spread across it. The full text gives the fossil accounts and the family analysis. The marsupials of Australia are a textbook case of evolution in isolation, and their oldest fossils anchor the timeline of that story.
plos-pone-0001958:
Myriam Rai and co-authors tested a drug fix for a nerve illness in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The illness, Friedreich ataxia, is passed down in families and harms both nerves and the heart. It stems from too little frataxin, a protein that works in the cell's power units, caused by a swollen repeat in the frataxin gene.

The team gave HDAC inhibitors, drugs that loosen the chemical marks that mute genes, to a mouse model of the illness. As the title states, the drugs corrected the frataxin shortage in the mice. If a muted gene can be coaxed back on, a drug path opens for an illness with no cure.
plos-pone-0002058:
Steven Schutzer and co-authors read the genome of a weakened form of a biothreat bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Burkholderia mallei causes glanders, which can be lethal in humans and animals, and it is little studied. Safety rules for listed agents have hampered research with it in many labs.

The team used whole genome sequencing to characterize a clinically attenuated strain, one that no longer causes full disease. If its genome proves it is truly weakened, the strain could be excluded from select agent lists. That would let more labs study glanders safely.
plos-pone-0002158:
Hendrik Harms, Konstantin Prass, Christian Meisel, and co-authors ran a clinical trial on preventing infection after stroke, published in PLOS ONE in 2008. Pneumonia is a leading cause of death after a major stroke. In mice, giving the antibiotic moxifloxacin early had prevented post-stroke infections, lowered deaths, and improved recovery.

The team tested the same idea in people with acute ischemic stroke, where a clot blocks blood flow to the brain. Patients were assigned by chance to preventive antibiotic therapy or standard care. Trials like this one decide whether a result seen in animals can be turned into a routine step that saves lives in the ward.
plos-pone-0002258:
Alison McGuigan, Derek Bruzewicz, Ana Glavan, and co-authors described a way to grow cells in tiny gel blocks, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cells behave differently on flat plastic than in the three-dimensional world of the body. Flat culture is still the most common method in biology, while 3D culture lacks a standard, easy form.

The team used replica molding to make sub-millimeter gel modules with cells sealed inside. The small blocks can be handled, stacked, and combined like building pieces. A simple standard for 3D culture could bring lab results closer to how cells truly behave inside tissues.
plos-pone-0002358:
Domingo Ojer Tsakiridu and co-authors surveyed factors linked to induced abortion among sex workers in Asturias, Spain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Their aim was to find what circumstances go together with having had an induced abortion in this group. The health needs of this group are often missed by standard services.

The team ran a cross-sectional study using a self-completion questionnaire answered by 212 women who attended the region's three sexually transmitted infection clinics. Mapping the factors that cluster with abortion helps those clinics target contraception advice, testing, and support to the women at highest risk.
plos-pone-0002458:
A research team led by Perfettini reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Jean-Luc Perfettini, Roberta Nardacci, Mehdi Bourouba, and others. Its subject is critical Involvement of the ATM-Dependent DNA Damage Response in the Apoptotic Demise of HIV-1-Elicited Syncytia. DNA damage can activate the oncosuppressor protein ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM), which phosphorylates the histone H2AX within characteristic DNA damage foci.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002558:
Work from Nishimura and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Tomoko Nishimura, Tamaki Ishima, Masaomi Iyo, and others. Its subject is potentiation of Nerve Growth Factor-Induced Neurite Outgrowth by Fluvoxamine. The title goes on to note role of Sigma-1 Receptors, IP 3 Receptors and Cellular Signaling Pathways. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have been widely used and are a major therapeutic advance in psychopharmacology.

However, their pharmacology is quite heterogeneous. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002658:
Pawan Gupta led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was PKCε stimulated arginine methylation of RIP140 for its Nuclear-Cytoplasmic export in adipocyte differentiation. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Pawan Gupta, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Receptor interacting protein 140 (RIP140) is a versatile transcriptional co-repressor that plays roles in diverse metabolic processes including fat accumulation in adipocytes. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002758:
Céline Lafourcade led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was regulation of the V-ATPase along the endocytic pathway occurs through reversible subunit association and membrane localization. The catalog record names Céline Lafourcade first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The lumen of endosomal organelles becomes increasingly acidic when going from the cell surface to lysosomes. The summary also notes a further point. Luminal pH thereby regulates important processes such as the release of internalized ligands from their receptor or the activation of lysosomal enzymes. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002858:
Morten Ruhwald led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was improving T-Cell assays for the diagnosis of latent TB infection: potential of a diagnostic test based on IP-10. Authorship is credited in the record to Morten Ruhwald and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. There is a need for simple tools such as the M.tuberculosis specific IFN-γ release assays (IGRA) to improve diagnosis of M.tuberculosis -infection in children. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002958:
Sofia Kring, Claus Holst, Esther Zimmermann and co-authors studied the fatness gene FTO across a wide range of body fat in 2008. A common variant in FTO, labeled rs9939609, is linked to total body fatness. What it does for fat placement and related metabolic traits was less clear.

The team checked the variant against abdominal and peripheral fat and obesity-linked traits in middle-aged men spanning a broad range of fatness. Published in PLOS ONE, the design shows whether the gene's effect grows, fades, or changes form as fatness rises. Such detail refines a headline gene link.
plos-pone-0003058:
José Cuevas, Manuela Torres-Puente, Nuria Jiménez-Hernández and co-authors tracked hepatitis C virus change around therapy in 2008. They analyzed selective forces on two genome regions thought to be involved in response to combined interferon plus ribavirin therapy. One region holds three hypervariable parts of the envelope E2 protein.

Comparing virus before and after combined therapy shows which sites selection pressed hardest. Published in PLOS ONE, such maps help explain treatment failure and resistance. Hepatitis C evolves fast within a patient, so therapy must be judged against a moving target. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003158:
K. Bretonnel Cohen, Martha Palmer and Lawrence Hunter study verb forms in biomedical writing in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They present data from the PennBioIE corpus on how common domain-specific verbs change their argument structure, and how their related noun forms behave. Alternation is the linguistics term for such shifts in the surface form of a verb.

Readers learn how biomedical verbs and their nominalizations vary in real text. That detail sounds narrow, but it matters for computer systems that mine medical papers for facts. Better handling of these forms means fewer errors when machines extract who did what to what.
plos-pone-0003258:
Amelia Cimmino, Rosanna Capasso, Fabbri Muller and colleagues study a repair enzyme in blood vessel cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural proteins undergo deamidation of certain asparagine residues in the body on their own, forming isoaspartyl residues. Deamidated, isomerized molecules are changed in both shape and how they work. The enzyme protein isoaspartate methyltransferase acts on such damage.

The title reports that this enzyme prevents apoptosis induced by oxidative stress in endothelial cells, with a role for Bcl-Xl deamidation and methylation. Readers see protein repair linked to cell survival under stress. Vessel lining protection matters in ageing and blood vessel disease.
plos-pone-0003358:
Jochen Brumm, Elizabeth Conibear, Wyeth W. Wasserman and colleagues present a method to find gene modules in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A central problem in systems biology research is identification and extension of biological modules, groups of genes or proteins participating in a common cellular process or physical complex. There is a persistent need for practical, principled methods to infer such modules from data.

Their approach discovers and expands gene modules by seeking isolated groups in a random graph process. Readers get an algorithm that grows modules from seeds while testing against randomness. Module maps help turn gene lists into working biological units.
plos-pone-0007458:
Guillaume Sapriel and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on diatoms, ocean algae that build glass-like shells from silicon. Diatoms produce much of the ocean's biological silica. Yet dissolved silicon can run short in surface waters and limit their growth. The team read activity across nearly the whole genome of one species, Phaeodactylum tricornutum, to see how it manages silicon.

They found that silicic acid transporters, the proteins that import silicon, are regulated at several levels at once. A network of genes responds as supply changes. That layered control lets the diatom adjust uptake to what the water offers. Because diatoms support a huge share of ocean life, their silicon handling matters globally. The study maps the control system behind it.
plos-pone-0007558:
Anne Spaulding and colleagues published an analysis in PLOS ONE in 2009 on HIV and AIDS among people in United States correctional facilities. Groups at high risk for HIV come together in prisons and jails, so infection rates there ran high early in the epidemic. The team assessed the share of the national epidemic borne by inmates and by people recently released, using 2006 data.

That share was declining, yet it remained disproportionately large. Because so many people pass through the correctional system, it stays a key public health setting. Testing, treatment, and prevention there reach people often missed elsewhere. The authors frame this as a persistent opportunity rather than only a burden. The analysis gives policymakers a measured picture of where the epidemic concentrates.
plos-pone-0007658:
Maud Mavigner and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on HIV that persists despite good treatment. Combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus, yet low-level production continues in many patients. The significance of that residual viremia was debated. The team characterized patients whose immune systems recovered poorly on therapy. They measured the lingering virus and the state of the patients' T cells together.

Residual viremia correlated with persistent T-cell activation in the poor responders. Restless T cells are a sign the immune system never fully calms. The lingering virus therefore looks like more than harmless background noise. It may help drive the incomplete recovery these patients show. The finding argues for watching low-level virus as a clinical signal. It also keeps the search for the virus's hiding places urgent.
plos-pone-0007758:
Nabarun Dasgupta and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks whether heavy news coverage of opioids tracks with more opioid deaths. Past research has linked media reporting to rises in drug abuse. Publicity has been suspected in usage swings for several drug classes.

The title poses the dilemma plainly: breaking the news, or fueling the epidemic? The authors test whether report volume and deaths rise and fall together in time. The answer matters for journalists and health officials. Coverage can warn the public, but it may also spread the behavior it describes.
plos-pone-0007858:
Marietta Dindo and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how group loyalty keeps foraging traditions alive in capuchin monkeys. Wild great apes are known for rich cultural repertoires and local traditions. Capuchins, among the brainiest monkeys, show traditions of their own.

The authors report that in-group conformity sustains different foraging traditions between groups. Monkeys copy their own group's way of finding food, even when other ways work. Conformity thus acts like cultural glue. The study extends the story of animal culture beyond the great apes. It also mirrors how human groups hold onto local customs.
plos-pone-0007958:
Jian Li and colleagues charted large DNA gains and losses in two population groups for PLOS ONE in 2009. Beyond single-letter changes, whole chunks of DNA can be copied extra times or lost, a pattern called copy number variation. The team mapped where such chunks fall across the genome.

Patterns differed between the Caucasian and Asian groups they studied. Those gaps add a layer of human diversity that letter-by-letter studies miss. A full chart of chunk changes helps explain trait and disease gaps between groups and improves how future gene hunts are planned.
plos-pone-0008058:
Cheng-Yeu Wu and colleagues gave a plain chemical account of the so-called nanobacteria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tiny granules found in blood were once hailed as living things of a wholly new kind. The team showed they are clumps of two blood proteins, fetuin-A and albumin, bound with calcium minerals.

The clumps form when the proteins both seed mineral growth and check it, a two-sided process the team rebuilt in the lab. No living thing is needed to explain the granules. Settling the claim frees research funds for real causes of the ills the granules were blamed for.
plos-pone-0008158:
Takeru Yoshimura and colleagues read the full immune signal mix in diseased eyes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The samples were vitreous fluid, the gel inside the eye, drawn from hundreds of patients. Many had diabetic eye disease, including macular swelling and advanced retinal damage.

Dozens of immune messengers were measured in each sample, and each disease carried its own pattern of highs and lows. Patterns that clean may one day let a fluid sample name the disease stage, or point to the messenger a drug should block to save sight.
plos-pone-0008258:
Klaus Kessler and colleagues studied a visual illusion in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. In the flash-lag effect, a flashed object seems to trail a moving one. The two are aligned in space, yet the flash looks behind. The effect has been replicated many times with simple stimuli. The team used biological motion, such as a moving person, for the first time.

They asked whether motor resonance predicts the pattern of the illusion. Motor resonance is the brain echoing observed movement in its own motor system. Links between resonance and the lag effect would tie perception to action. The study extends a classic illusion to human movement.
plos-pone-0008358:
Simon C. F. Rawlinson and colleagues compared adult rat bones in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Limb fractures and bone loss cause growing harm in ageing populations. Weight-bearing limbs lose bone with age, yet the skull vault keeps its mass. Why regions differ was the question behind the study. Bones carry markers of their developmental origin.

Adult rat bones maintained distinct regional expression of those markers. In other words, bones remember where they came from. That memory may explain why skull and limb respond differently to ageing. It could also shape treatments for bone loss.
plos-pone-0008458:
Maria Murholm and co-authors track genes in brown fat cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Brown fat cells burn energy to make heat. White fat cells store energy instead. The split rests in part on mitochondria, the cell's power units. Brown cells hold a protein that lets them waste energy as heat. The team watch cells as they mature in mice.

They measure genes that copy and read mitochondrial DNA. Those genes shift as brown cells form and are recruited. The pattern shows how the power system is built for heat making. It helps explain how brown fat turns on when needed.
plos-pone-0008558:
Kathleen McClendon and co-authors compare tumor suppressor paths in mouse cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. RB and p53 are tumor suppressors that mediate responses to DNA damage. Loss of both together is common in human cancers. Surprisingly, how they cooperate in damage signaling was still enigmatic. That cooperation bears on tumor formation and on response to therapy. The team use a mouse primary cell model to separate their effects.

Inactivating each path has a differential impact on damage response. It also changes how therapy can transform cells into cancerous ones. Knowing which suppressor is lost may predict treatment effects. The work clarifies a common but poorly understood cancer genotype.
plos-pone-0008658:
Giulia Spigoni and co-authors study antisense regulation in mouse brains in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Emx2 encodes a transcription factor expressed in embryonic tissues and the central nervous system. It is implicated in cerebral cortex development, including field specification and precursor proliferation. Antisense transcripts are RNA copies read from the opposite DNA strand. They can regulate the sense gene that shares their locus. The team characterize antisense transcripts at the Emx2 locus in cortico-cerebral precursors.

They find those transcripts regulate Emx2 expression in those precursors. Tuning Emx2 levels shapes how cortex areas are specified. Antisense control adds a fine dial to a master developmental gene. The work may illuminate cortical malformations linked to Emx2.
plos-pone-0008758:
Brian Onken and Monica Driscoll asked whether a diabetes drug can lengthen healthy life in worms. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Metformin is a widely used drug for type-2 diabetes. Reports hinted it extends healthy years in mice without diabetes. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans offered fast genetics to find the mechanism. The team suspected the drug mimics eating less.

Worms on metformin stayed healthy longer than untreated worms. The benefit ran through AMPK and LKB1, energy sensors in cells. It also needed SKN-1, a stress-response switch. Those links tie drug action to the same circuits as dietary restriction.
plos-pone-0008858:
David Gómez-Varela, Tobias Kohl, Manuela Schmidt, and colleagues filmed single channel proteins wandering in rat brain cell membranes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Eag1 is a voltage-gated channel shaping nerve cell firing. Channels must reach and leave synapses at the right times. Watching native channels move in real time was long impossible. Quantum dots, tiny glowing crystals, changed that.

Dots attached to single Eag1 channels lit their paths across the membrane. Tracking revealed how fast and how far the channels roam. Movement rules help explain how synapses tune their strength. The method opens other native proteins to the same filming.
plos-pone-0008958:
Karin Loser and colleagues showed a skin pigment hormone also helps build killer immune cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The hormone, alpha-MSH, is best known for darkening skin colour. It also plays roles in appetite, sexual function, and calming inflammation. The team asked whether it shapes CD8 T cells, the immune cells that kill infected cells.

In mice and in human cells, the hormone proved necessary for these T cells to develop properly. Without its signal, the cytotoxic cells matured poorly. The finding adds an immune duty to a hormone long filed under skin biology. It may matter for vaccines or treatments that rely on strong killer T cells.
plos-pone-0009058:
Sevin Turcan, Donna Slonim, and Douglas Vetter followed ear development in mice missing one hearing receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The missing piece is the alpha9 nicotinic receptor in the cochlea. Without it, the ear loses a whole channel of nerve control. Synapse structures at the hair cells also form abnormally.

The team profiled gene activity over time in the mutant mice. Cochlear maturation slowed compared with normal mice. Meanwhile parts of the calming GABA system ramped up, perhaps in compensation. The timeline shows how one missing receptor reshapes an entire sense organ.
plos-pone-0009158:
Daniel Datiko and Bernt Lindtjørn priced community-based tuberculosis care in Ethiopia, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ethiopia lacked hard numbers on what TB control costs to deliver in practice. Health extension workers are community staff trained to give basic care locally. A community trial had these workers treat smear-positive TB patients near their homes.

The analysis measured the full cost per patient treated in this way. It also judged cost-effectiveness against the standard clinic-based route. Care delivered in the community can spare patients long, costly trips. For a poor health system, the price tag decides whether such schemes can scale.
plos-pone-0009258:
Alexis Dumortier and co-authors published this mouse skin study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Notch pathway guides skin cells to mature properly as embryos develop. Removing Notch signaling from young skin breaks the skin barrier. It also triggers a blood disorder in mice, which raised questions about adult skin.

The team removed Notch signaling from the skin of mice and watched what followed. The mice developed a disease like atopic dermatitis, the itchy rash of eczema. Alongside it came a lethal overgrowth of myeloid blood cells. The double result ties one signaling pathway to both skin health and blood cell control.
plos-pone-0009358:
Kerryl Piper and co-authors published this orthopedics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two blood tests, CRP and ESR, help doctors spot infections around artificial joints. They are well proven for infected hip and knee replacements. Far less was known about their value for shoulder replacements or spine implants.

The team reviewed patients facing revision or removal of shoulder and spine hardware. They checked how well the two tests flagged real infections there. Knowing a test's limits in each body site prevents both missed infections and needless surgery. The study extends the evidence for two cheap, common tests into less-studied territory.
plos-pone-0011458:
Manju Mamtani and co-authors searched in 2010 for gene patterns that predict the course of Kawasaki disease in Japanese children. The disease brings fever and inflamed blood vessels in young children, and in the worst cases it scars the coronary arteries of the heart. Standard treatment with IVIG helps most children, but some respond poorly for unknown reasons.

The team linked variants in two immune receptor genes and the copy number of a related gene to the disease itself, to heart artery damage, and to IVIG response. Those clues could one day help doctors spot, at diagnosis, which children need the most aggressive care. For a disease whose worst harm is preventable with timely treatment, a genetic warning system would be a genuine clinical gain.
plos-pone-0011558:
Hediye Nese Cinar and co-authors showed in 2010 that one cholera toxin does the damage in a tiny worm host. Vibrio cholerae, the cholera germ, makes several candidate weapons, and the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans offers a simple gut in which to test them. The team fed worms the bacterium with and without its hemolysin, a toxin that punctures cell membranes.

Without hemolysin, the germ lost its power to kill the worms, delay their development, and riddle their intestines with vacuoles, hollow damaged pockets. The toxin is therefore required, not incidental, for this harm. A worm model turns a human pathogen's weapon into a trait that can be screened quickly and cheaply. Compounds or bacterial mutations that disarm hemolysin can now be hunted at a scale human-relevant models cannot match.
plos-pone-0011658:
Peter Kraft and co-authors studied a clotting regulator called TAFI in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clot formation is a key step in ischaemic stroke, when a clot blocks blood flow in the brain. Thrombin, a central clotting enzyme, also activates TAFI, which slows the breakdown of clots and makes them more stable.

Mice lacking TAFI might therefore have been expected to fare better. Instead, they proved susceptible to clots and ischaemic injury in the brain. The surprise vulnerability reveals a protective side to TAFI in cerebral blood flow that simple clot logic would not predict.
plos-pone-0011758:
Young-Sang Koh and co-authors tested a frontline immune sensor against tick-borne germs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ehrlichiae are tiny germs that live inside host cells and cause human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis, a rising and at times fatal tick-borne disease. The part played by fast innate sensing, as opposed to later adaptive defence, needed defining.

Working in mice, the team showed signals through the sensor MyD88 add a great deal to host defence against ehrlichial infection. Without it, control of the germs suffered. Pinning down this sensor's role sharpens the picture of the first line of defence against a little-known infection.
plos-pone-0011858:
Jan Zietsch and co-authors studied in 2010 a stretch of extra DNA found in a rare and deadly nerve tumor. These tumors grow from Schwann cells, which wrap around nerves, and they show up in about one in ten people who have the gene fault called neurofibromatosis type 1. Care is hard and life spans are short, so new drug ideas are badly needed.

The extra DNA sits in one small part of chromosome 4 and holds genes that run too hot in the tumors. One of those genes is a known target of the drug sunitinib, so the team asked what the extra copies mean for that drug. Tying a tumor's DNA faults to a drug now in use is one of the fastest ways to find help for rare cancers.
plos-pone-0011958:
Michael Graf, Alessandro Cellerino, and Christoph Englert kept in 2010 a short-lived African fish with the sexes apart to see what changes. Life history theory treats mating as costly: energy spent on reproduction cannot be spent on growth or survival. The turquoise killifish, Nothobranchius furzeri, lives fast and is a favorite aging model.

Females housed without males grew larger, yet their lifespan did not improve. Growth and longevity thus came apart: removing mating costs bought size, not time. That split is a useful check on simple trade-off stories, and it helps aging researchers choose what to measure in this much-used fish.
plos-pone-0012058:
Kenta Nakamura and co-workers studied in 2010 the small RNAs guiding a famous regeneration trick: the newt regrowing its own lens. After lens removal, pigment cells of the dorsal iris change identity and build a new lens; cells of the ventral iris cannot. MicroRNAs, tiny gene regulators, were candidates for enforcing that difference.

The team found microRNAs specifically controlling cell proliferation during regeneration, plus evidence that these regulators work in networks rather than alone. A network view matters because regeneration is a program, not a single switch. Newts remain the champions of vertebrate regeneration, and their small-RNA score is one of the few readable parts of that program.
plos-pone-0012158:
Yong Woo, Michael Walker, and Gary Churchill studied how genes are arranged along mammalian genomes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gene order is not random: genes that switch on together often sit near each other in clusters. Why the genome keeps that arrangement, and what mechanisms maintain it, were the open questions behind their analysis.

The authors characterized these shared-expression neighborhoods across mammalian genomes and probed what creates them. Clusters may help the cell coordinate whole programs from a few control points. Understanding this layout adds a layer to genetics beyond single genes, pointing at the genome as an organized city rather than a parts list.
plos-pone-0012258:
Phillip Lord and Robert Stevens argued for grounding biological ontologies in how things really are, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ontologies, formal dictionaries that let computers reason about biology, now underpin databases across the field. They are used to describe everything from genes to anatomy, and models built on them drive real research decisions.

The risk, the authors argue, is ontologies drifting into tidy logic that misdescribes messy living things. Adding a little reality means checking formal categories against actual biology, including its exceptions and gray zones. For infrastructure this widely used, small distortions multiply through thousands of studies, so the call for realism is practical, not philosophical.
plos-pone-0012358:
Hyo-Jeong Lee, Seung-Ae Kim, Hyo-Jung Lee and co-workers tested a plant-derived compound against tumor blood vessel growth in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Paeonol comes from the root bark of a peony used in East Asian medicine, and earlier work showed it can slow new vessel growth. The team made a changed form, paeonol oxime, and asked how strongly it blocks vessels fed by growth signals.

In cell tests, the compound curbed vessel growth driven by the signal bFGF and lowered levels of VEGF, another vessel signal, in fibrosarcoma cells. Tumors need new vessels to grow, so blocking two signals at once is promising. The study adds a candidate to the search for gentler anti-cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0012458:
Hari Raghu, Sajani Lakka, Christopher Gondi and colleagues blocked two proteins to cut vessel growth signals in tumors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The proteins uPA and uPAR help glioma brain tumors build blood vessels, guided by another factor called angiogenin. Earlier work by the group showed silencing the pair slowed vessel growth in glioma cells.

Here they extended the test to vessel-lining cells and glioblastoma lines, and silencing the pair again blunted angiogenin's push. Tumors starved of new vessels grow more slowly. The combined evidence makes the uPA-uPAR pair a candidate target for anti-vessel therapy in aggressive brain tumors.
plos-pone-0012558:
Pablo Fernandez, Stéphane Petres, Salaheddine Mécheri and colleagues tested an antibody-like blocker of placental malaria, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In pregnancy-associated malaria, infected red cells stick to a placental receptor called CSA, endangering mother and baby. The parasite protein Var2CSA does the sticking, and one of its domains, DBL5 epsilon, is a vaccine candidate.

Immune responses raised against that domain blocked infected cells from sticking to placenta-derived cells under flowing conditions that mimic blood flow. Blocking across parasite strains — strain-transcendent protection — is the hard requirement for any malaria vaccine. Passing the flow test moves this domain closer to real candidacy.
plos-pone-0012658:
Khiabanian, Holmes, Kelly and co-authors mined hospital records for early signs of the 2009 flu pandemic. Health officials declared a flu pandemic in mid 2009, the first one of the new century. By July, New York-Presbyterian Hospital in New York City was seeing its effects firsthand.

Their 2010 study searched the hospital's electronic records for patterns that marked the pandemic's arrival. Patient records, gathered for care, can double as an early warning system for outbreaks. Showing that in a real hospital helps cities plan faster responses to the next pandemic.  Record patterns were checked against the known pandemic timeline.
plos-pone-0012758:
Thaker, Vanak, Owen and co-authors watched how zebra and wildebeest groups shift in wooded savanna. Herd animals in open grasslands have been studied for decades, and grouping there trades food access against safety from predators. Woodland changes that trade, since trees block sight lines and ambush cover is everywhere.

Their 2010 field study measured group sizes and movement as risk and habitat density changed across the woodland. The herds adjusted their grouping in ways grassland studies would not predict. Results like these refine how ecologists model prey behaviour across whole landscapes.
pmc-1781458:
Provenzano, Eliceiri, Campbell, and co-authors study how collagen is rearranged where a breast tumour meets nearby tissue. Links between the tumour lining and its supporting tissue matter greatly in the breast. When those links go wrong, cancer can form and begin to invade.

Dense collagen in breast tissue is known to raise the risk of breast cancer. The team examined how fibres line up at the tumour edge and how that layout affects local spread. Their findings link fibre patterns to invasion, suggesting the tissue around a tumour helps decide how far it travels.
pmc-2933358:
Kumarasamy, Toleman, Walsh, and co-authors report the emergence of a new antibiotic resistance mechanism called NDM-1. Certain gut bacteria carrying this trait resist carbapenems, a class of last-resort antibiotics. The authors warn that such bacteria could become a major world health problem.

They investigated how common NDM-1 was among drug-resistant bacteria in India, Pakistan, and the United Kingdom, using molecular, biological, and epidemiological methods. Finding the trait across countries showed resistance genes can travel with patients and shape treatment far from their origin.  Travel-linked cases in Britain showed the trait had already crossed borders quietly.
pmc-3738458:
Lawrence, Huber, Pages, and co-authors describe Bioconductor infrastructure for computing with annotated genomic ranges. Genomic data are naturally expressed as ranges: stretches of DNA along a chromosome, each carrying labels and values. Their software represents and computes on such ranges inside the R statistics environment.

Three packages sit at the core: IRanges, GenomicRanges, and a third integrating them with experiments. That foundation lets many other tools share one data language. Standard range infrastructure quietly powers thousands of genomic analyses, from sequencing pipelines to genome browsers.  Range operations such as overlap and counting form the grammar of genomic analysis.
pmc-4556158:
Kang, Froula, Egan, and their team presented MetaBAT in 2015 for metagenome work. A metagenome holds DNA from a whole community of microbes mixed together. Grouping assembled fragments into bins, one per organism, lets researchers study single species from that mixture.

MetaBAT was built to reconstruct single genomes from complex communities in an efficient and accurate way. Earlier binning tools struggled with the tangled nature of real communities. Better bins reveal organisms that cannot be grown in the lab, along with their roles. That advances studies of oceans, soils, and the human gut, where most microbes remain uncultured.
pmc-7919858:
Jennifer Dan and co-authors measured in 2021 how long immune memory to SARS-CoV-2 lasts after infection. Knowing the durability of that memory matters for vaccine design, for testing, and for predicting the pandemic's future course. The team examined several parts of immune memory at once, including antibodies and memory cells that can reactivate on a new encounter.

Their samples came from nearly two hundred confirmed cases, with follow up reaching about eight months after infection. They report that most parts of immune memory were still detectable at that point, though levels varied between people. The findings calmed early fears that protection might fade within weeks, while leaving open how memory performs over years.
plos-pone-0360158:
Johannes Aengenheyster, Olav Velthuis, and Alex van Venrooij examined in 2026 what the private museums of wealthy economic elites contribute to the arts. Rich collectors increasingly open museums of their own rather than only donating to public ones. The authors ask whether these institutions are mere bandwagons, fashionable copies of one another, or genuine breeding grounds for artistic innovation.

Their study weighs what private museums add: new exhibition space, support for living artists, and public access to collections that would otherwise stay hidden. It also weighs the concerns, including private taste shaping public culture. The question matters for cultural policy, since cities court such museums while public institutions compete with them for art and attention.
plos-pone-0358558:
Jing Yang, Zhenqing Li, and Yoshinori Yamaguchi studied in 2026 whether teaching by outcomes makes engineering students more skilled. The approach is called outcome based education. It plans a course backward, from the skills students should be able to show at the end, rather than forward from a list of topics. Their test bed was a course on intelligent control, a hard subject about smart control systems.

The team used mixed methods, joining test scores and skill checks with what students and teachers said about the course. Book learning alone does not prove skill in such a subject, so the checks asked students to do real tasks. If planning by outcomes builds real skill here, the case grows for using it across engineering degrees.
plos-pone-0360658:
Wei Li, Ming Ma, and Jinyue Lu studied in 2026 how the Chinese public judged a cultural heritage scandal across different online platforms. The controversy concerned artifacts donated to the Nanjing Museum and how they were handled. The authors used topic modeling, a computational method that finds themes in large volumes of text, to map what people actually talked about on each platform.

Public judgment in a heritage crisis shapes whether a museum keeps the trust that brings donors and visitors. Comparing platforms shows how the same facts become different stories in different online rooms. Their study offers museums and cultural agencies a method for listening during a crisis, and a record of how this one unfolded.
plos-pone-0359858:
Álvaro Huerta Ojeda and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on aging and function. It studies community-dwelling older adults, people living in their own homes rather than care facilities. The authors examine the association between the muscle quality index and the time needed to rise from lying face down to standing.

Rising from the floor is a real-world test of strength that matters after a fall. A muscle quality index condenses how much force muscle produces for its size. If the index tracks floor-rise time, clinicians gain a simple screen for older adults losing independence, and exercise programs gain a target.
plos-pone-0358258:
Micah Vinet and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on eye diagnosis. It presents software that automatically measures the thickness of the cornea's central surface layer, the epithelium. The purpose is diagnosing limbal stem cell deficiency, a failure of the cells that renew the cornea's surface.

When limbal stem cells fail, the cornea clouds and vision suffers, yet the condition is hard to measure by eye alone. Automated thickness readings could make diagnosis more objective and repeatable between clinics. Corneal specialists evaluating surface disease are the readers who would use such measurements in practice.
plos-pone-0357258: Xu, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on keeping coal mine roadways dry and safe. The work searches for the best settings for roadway supports that block water. The search used an algorithm the author calls FFA. Getting support design right guards miners from flooding and roof falls. The study speaks to engineers who plan supports in wet ground conditions.
plos-pone-0354958: Sakthivel and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a material for storing electric charge. The material is BaMoO4, a metal oxide used in supercapacitors, devices that charge and discharge quickly. The team varied how long the material cooked in hot water and tracked changes in shape and performance. Their tests used an asymmetric supercapacitor setup. Small shape changes can shift how much energy such devices hold.
plos-pone-0358858: Tufael and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how insulin resistance may help liver cancer grow. Part of the work is computer-based, modeling how a protein called IRS-1 meets the core protein of hepatitis C virus, genotype 3. The virus and insulin resistance often occur together. If the link holds, it could explain part of the cancer risk carried by infected patients.
plos-pone-0358958: Bíl and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on road deaths in Czechia across more than five decades. Autopsy records from 1969 to 2024 covered people killed while walking, cycling, or otherwise unprotected. The title reports that these deaths come with greater trauma than other road deaths. Long records like these show whether safety laws and car design have truly protected the most exposed road users.
plos-pone-0359158:
Madeline Fernandez-Pineda and five colleagues study what miscarriage care felt like during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Pandemic rules kept support people out of clinics and disrupted appointments, adding strain to an already painful loss. The authors combined surveys and interviews to capture both the numbers and the women's own accounts of that period.

Seventy-one women in North Carolina who miscarried during stay at home mandates took part, and eighteen gave long interviews. About half rated their care experience as poor. Pandemic hardships such as missing support persons were similar across groups, but women with poor experiences reported clearly higher stress, anxiety, and depression. Among those treated with medicine or surgery, a good care experience went together with lower distress.
europmc-pmc7337658: Doctors and scientists took on global testing of echocardiography in patients in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7794558: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on deep learning (layered computer learning)-enabled medical computer vision. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8825858: Zhang and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on the control, function, and role of lipophagy, a form of selective autophagy (cell self-cleanup), in metabolic (energy-use) illnesses. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc7257158: Doctors and scientists took on CCL2/CCR2 signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) in cancer pathogenesis (how the disease develops) in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-958: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at transportation Security: TSA Has Developed a Risk-Based Covert Testing Program, but Could Better Mitigate Aviation Security Vulnerabilities Identified Through C. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
europmc-pmc8791758: A fresh look at a common feature of pesticides: oxidative stress (cell damage from unstable oxygen)-the role of cell damage from unstable oxygen in pesticide-induced toxicity arrived with this 2022 research paper. Pesticides are important chemicals or biological (from living things) agents that deter or kill pests. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc7003858: A fresh look at t-cell exhaustion arrived with this 2019 research paper. The t-cell reply is central in the adaptive immune-driven elimination of germ-infected and/or cancer cells. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7408158: A 2020 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at interleukin (immune messenger)-1β and cancer. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8470858: Doctors and scientists took on the effects and mechanisms (the inner workings) of probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and postbiotics on metabolic (energy-use) diseases aimed at gut in this 2021 review paper. It walks through what the field currently knows, study by study. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc9279158: Doctors and scientists took on single-cell (one cell at a time) and bulk transcriptome sequencing (reading DNA letter by letter) identifies two epithelial tumor cell states in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7734058: Doctors and scientists took on circrna hsa_circrna_104348 boosts liver carcinoma (a common type of cancer) progression (worsening) through modulating miR-187-3p/RTKN2 axis and activating wnt/β-catenin pathway in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc8850458: A fresh look at the AUTOTAC chemical biology platform for aimed protein degradation via the autophagy (cell self-cleanup)-lysosome system arrived with this 2022 research paper. Aimed protein degradation allows aimed at undruggable proteins for treatment uses as well as eliminating proteins. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9321158: Doctors and scientists took on the movement illness society criteria for the diagnosis of multiple system atrophy in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Better ways to spot trouble early give doctors a head start on treatment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-258: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on aviation Weather: FAA Is Reevaluating Services at Key Centers; Both FAA and the National Weather Service Need to Better Ensure Product Quality. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
europmc-pmc7125958: A 2020 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at biosynthesis and biology of mammalian gpi-anchored proteins. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc6990758: A 2020 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at clinical (in patients) evidence for link of acupuncture and acupressure with improved cancer pain: a systematic review (a review of every study). It combines data from many other studies to reach a firmer answer. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc9408758: Doctors and scientists took on the pivotal role of nf-kb in the pathogenesis (how the disease develops) and therapeutics (treatments) of Alzheimer's disease in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc9805458: A fresh look at body-worn and flexible electric sensors for sweat analysis: a review arrived with this 2023 review paper. Flexible body-worn sweat sensors allow continuous, real-time, noninvasive spotting of sweat analytes, provide insight into human physiology at the level. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc7221158: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on the tumor microenvironment (the tissue surrounding a tumor) in the reply to immune checkpoint blockade therapies. plos-pone-0348858:
Russell Tronstad and Ibrahima Sall valued education programs for people with limited resources, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Extension programs teach farming and life skills, but they must prove their worth to funders and to the audiences themselves. The authors used a willingness-to-accept experiment, asking what payment people would accept in place of the teaching.

Tronstad and Sall's valuations put hard numbers on what participants judge the education to be worth. Program planners can compare those values with costs when deciding what to offer. The method respects the audience's own judgment instead of assuming benefit. For services aimed at low-income communities, that respect, backed by numbers, strengthens the case for funding what truly helps.
plos-pone-0357758:
Nazia Fairooz Alam led a team of eight authors designing a vaccine candidate on the computer, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Human metapneumovirus is a lung virus with no vaccine yet. The team used reverse vaccinology and pan-genomic methods to predict a candidate built from multiple epitopes, the parts of the virus the immune system recognizes.

Alam's in silico design gives vaccine developers a concrete head start instead of a blank page. Computer prediction cannot prove a vaccine works; it narrows the search to designs worth making and testing. Pan-genomic input helps the candidate cover many virus strains at once. For a virus that burdens children and older adults each winter, a faster start matters.
plos-pone-0357958:
Guangjun Liu led a team of five authors designing a lean part for vision models, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Attention modules help a model focus on the right parts of an image, but they usually add parameters that cost memory and speed. Their module, PSAFM, fuses features across space with attention, yet adds no parameters at all.

Liu's parameter-free design boosts accuracy without the usual bloat, making it cheap to drop into existing networks. Small models for phones and cameras benefit most, since every parameter counts there. A part that improves many models, rather than one bespoke system, spreads its value widely. The study is a reminder that clever structure can beat brute size in machine learning design.
plos-pone-0343858:
Xuejing Fu, Zhen Chen, and Wentao Lu built a test for AI systems on drug regulation, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rules for medicines differ sharply between China and the United States, and AI assistants giving regulatory advice must handle both. Their benchmark, Sino-US-DrugQA, evaluates large language models on cross-border pharmaceutical regulation questions.

Fu's test reveals which AI systems navigate the regulatory maze and which stumble. Companies use language models for drafting and compliance help, where a confident wrong answer can be costly. A public benchmark lets buyers compare systems on the same hard questions. It also pushes model builders to improve on legal and regulatory knowledge, a weak spot for general-purpose AI.
plos-pone-0357458:
Jianqi Guo and Yingmei Qu compare two kinds of academic English writing in a 2026 language study. One set comes from Chinese students training as translators, and the other from native English academic writers. Using two collections the authors built themselves, they measured sentence build with a standard software tool that tracks clause and phrase patterns.

Trainee writing leaned on longer clauses, joined phrases, and heavy noun groups, while native writing used more layered clauses packed into each unit. The groups differed clearly on most of the measures tested. Guo and Qu link the gap to second-language growth, pressure from the source text, and translation habits, and they point teachers toward training that builds clause-level skill.
plos-pone-0357658:
Masanori Nakajo and colleagues test whether an advanced CT measure can grade worn spinal disks without relying only on standard scans. Disk wear is the most common source of low back pain, and MRI grading is the usual reference. In about one hundred patients who had both scan types, the team measured several signals in the disk's tough rim and soft center across several hundred lumbar disks.

Plain CT values and the new density measure moved in opposite directions in rim and center as MRI wear grades rose. The gap in density between front rim and center tracked wear grade most strongly of all. Nakajo and colleagues say spectral CT density could help grade disk wear when MRI is unavailable or unclear, adding a quantitative option to routine spine imaging.
plos-pone-0354458:
Guanlin Dai, Da Gao, and Chao Zheng improve how AI finds a requested moment inside a video, a task called moment retrieval. Standard transformer models hunt the whole video at once because their search prompts carry no built-in sense of time span, and they falter on events of varied length. The team replaces those loose prompts with bell-shaped time priors that have a learnable center and width, seeded from local video features at several scales.

On a standard public benchmark, the design clearly helped one weak spot: finding long events, where scores rose by about two points over a leading rival with statistical support. Overall recall differences stayed inconclusive. Dai and colleagues present the prior as a cheap, focused part for studying scale-aware search in video models.
plos-pone-0357158:
Wenjie Sun and co-authors build a repeatable traffic monitoring workflow for highways that lack road sensors, testing it on a Sarawak stretch of the Pan Borneo Highway, in Malaysian Borneo. Probe data from navigation platforms can fill the gap if handled carefully. Their pipeline collects platform car data on a schedule, cleans it by fixed rules, stores it, computes pressure indicators, and cross-checks one platform against another over an overlapping month.

One platform's panel stayed available nearly all the time and caught a repeated evening pressure build-up at the same hour. The two platforms told similar stories at matched times and places. Sun and colleagues caution that probe data is not ground truth, but argue it can keep sparse corridors under steady watch.
plos-pone-0356258:
Yuling Cui and co-authors developed a freeze-dried DNA profiling kit. It removes forensic testing's dependence on freezers. Their 2026 paper describes a six-color fluorescent reagent. It covers twenty-nine identity markers plus a sex marker. The mix is engineered with a hardy enzyme and protective additives. So the dried reagent survives at room temperature. It wakes instantly when water is added.

In validation, the kit detected full profiles from tiny DNA amounts. It stayed stable for two months on the shelf. It also tolerated common contaminants. Head-to-head against liquid reagents, it matched identification rates exactly. It handled trace samples better. A pocketable, ready-to-use kit could bring reliable DNA identification to crime scenes, disaster zones, and small rural laboratories.
plos-pone-0348158:
Mark Cortnage, Joseph Lillis, and Justin Roberts sat twenty-four men down in focus groups to talk frankly about dieting, a world most weight loss programs design for women. Their 2026 qualitative study, involving men mostly in their forties with overweight or obesity, sorted the conversation into themes about perceptions, barriers, turning points, and what makes change stick.

The men described dieting as cyclical and faintly embarrassing, driven by misinformation and low expectations, with appearance, more than health, supplying the spark to start. Three supports stood out: a buddy, a mentor, and above all a partner at home. The authors argue programs recruiting men should build that buddy, mentor, and spousal scaffolding in from the start rather than handing over a diet sheet.
plos-pone-0356358:
Guoqin Wang and colleagues sifted blood gene data from heart attack patients for genes where two destructive processes meet: macrophage-driven inflammation and ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Their 2026 bioinformatics study merged two public datasets, corrected the batch differences between them with unusual care, and published this as a revised analysis with tightened false-positive controls.

Seven candidate genes survived the intersection, and five were confirmed raised in follow-up laboratory tests. Whole-genome pattern checks pointed at inflammatory and oxidative stress programs, and immune signatures shifted most clearly for neutrophils. Because the candidate network proved too sparse for hub claims, the authors present the seven as prioritized leads for heart attack biology rather than established drivers.
plos-pone-0346758:
Maureen O'Callaghan and colleagues interviewed five frail older adults living with urinary incontinence. Five family caregivers joined them. The topic was treatments for a condition that is common, burdensome, and quietly endured. Their 2026 study explored how participants view conservative, drug, and surgical options. This perspective is rarely gathered from this group.

Five themes emerged. People managed alone with pads and routines until those failed. Many believed leakage is simply what ageing is, a fatalism that blocked help-seeking. New treatments raised fears of adding to caregivers' loads. Invasive options drew reluctance. Yet both patients and caregivers were cautiously willing to try gentle conservative approaches. The authors say acceptance hinges on dignity, burden, and shaking the myth that leakage is fate.
plos-pone-0356758:
Zhengyao Che and colleagues surveyed 305 women undergoing IVF treatment at a hospital in Yunnan, China, about their sexual function, a side of fertility care clinics seldom ask about. Their 2026 study scored function with a standard index, measured psychological distress, and used latent profile analysis to let natural patient groupings emerge rather than imposing cutoffs.

Three groups appeared: about a fifth with low function, two fifths in the middle, and the rest doing well. Younger, better-educated, and more distressed women clustered in the middle group, city residents in the good group, and longer infertility with more past pregnancies predicted the low group. The profiles give clinics a screening shortcut for an intimate problem that quietly strains couples already under treatment stress.
plos-pone-0355558:
Christian Jäger and three colleagues describe how a German university medical center moved its lab record-keeping from paper to a digital notebook system, reporting in 2026. The open-source platform they adopted promises better data quality and easier sharing, but such switches often stall on user habits. Their study combines the rollout story with a survey of researchers about how they actually document their work.

Most survey respondents were experienced researchers, yet many complained that documenting took too long, was badly organized, and made old information hard to find. Nearly everyone named ease of use as the top requirement, with training and ongoing support close behind. Over the rollout period the platform grew to hundreds of users across dozens of teams. The authors share checklists and helper apps so other institutions can copy the approach.
plos-pone-0356058:
Liang He and co-authors tested whether plant and plastic fibres can protect swelling soil in regions with hard winter freezing. Expansive soil swells and shrinks with moisture, and freeze-thaw cycles damage it further. Their 2026 study mixed polypropylene and lignin fibres into such soil and ran swelling, strength, and freezing tests.

Lignin fibre alone performed best overall, cutting swelling most and raising shear strength most. Adding polypropylene fibre on top improved strength further. After repeated freeze-thaw cycles, the mixed-fibre soil lost far less strength than untreated soil. Microscope images showed fibres bridging and overlapping inside the soil, which explains the gains. The authors present fibre mixing as a practical fix for building on difficult ground.
plos-pone-0336758:
Shizuka Hashimoto and co-authors tested how bait choice shapes fish surveys that read DNA from river water. In species-rich tropical rivers, the short DNA tags used to trigger copying can miss whole groups. Their 2026 study worked in Brazil's Teles Pires basin, comparing standard and modified tag pairs against global and local reference libraries.

One modified tag pair detected the most species under every library setup. Combining libraries widened detection further, and a locally built library, drawn from fish actually caught nearby, added species that global lists missed. Hashimoto and colleagues conclude that tag choice and reference quality together decide what an environmental DNA survey can honestly claim to find.
plos-pone-0355958:
Maarten Mosch and colleagues reviewed a rare knee-area fracture seen in teenagers at a Dutch trauma centre. The tibial tubercle, where the thigh tendon anchors below the knee, can crack during sport while bones are still growing. Their 2026 series covered forty young patients treated over fifteen years.

Nearly all patients were boys, injured mostly during sports, at an average age of about fourteen. Most fractures needed surgery, usually screw fixation; the rest healed without an operation. Complications were uncommon, at about one in ten fractures, and no compartment syndrome occurred. Mosch and colleagues offer the series as practical guidance for a rare injury that youth sports are making more familiar.
plos-pone-0354258:
Nazlı Yanar Tunçel and Züleyha Avşar gave seventh-grade students virtual reality games for eight weeks of physical education and tested their balance and coordination. Schools are weighing headsets as teaching tools, but physical effects need evidence. Their 2026 experiment compared twenty headset students with nineteen controls on standard movement batteries.

The headset group improved more on backward balancing, side-to-side jumping, and platform transport tasks. Total coordination scores and balance reach in both directions also favoured the players. One test, single-leg hopping, showed no group difference. Yanar Tunçel and Avşar conclude that well-chosen virtual games can train real body skills, while noting that not every skill responds equally.
plos-pone-0355858:
Proshenjit Sarker and S M Shamsul Alam built a three-stage vision cascade that reads Bangladeshi vehicle license plates. Plate recognition feeds traffic enforcement, but Bangla plates vary widely and older character-reading tools cover too few symbol classes. Their 2026 system chains three detection models, each solving one step.

The first model finds vehicles, the second locates the plate, and the third reads characters directly, with no separate text-recognition engine. Its character set spans one hundred four classes, covering city codes, vehicle types, and digits. Training used more than nine thousand images, with a held-out set for external checking. Sarker and Alam aim for a recogniser shaped to local plates rather than adapted from foreign ones.
plos-pone-0355158:
Nigatu Madebo, Feleke Yareshe, and Lebsework Lemma propose in 2026 a new controller to guide unmanned aircraft along a set path more closely. They first recorded how a fuzzy logic controller behaved, then trained a combined neural and fuzzy system on those records. The trained system can adjust its own settings during flight, unlike the fixed original.

Simulations covered normal flight, flight with outside pushes, and flight when aircraft traits changed. The new controller cut a standard tracking error score sharply in the harder cases and by a smaller margin in normal flight. The authors present the method for jobs needing precise, steady flight.
plos-pone-0354158:
Matthew Davitt and co-authors map in 2026 research that uses muscle electrical recording to judge the physical strain on surgeons doing keyhole and robot assisted belly surgery. Their scoping review followed standard guidance and searched many databases for studies in real or simulated surgical settings. Close to a hundred studies spanning nearly three decades qualified.

Most work covered plain keyhole surgery, with far fewer robot studies. Shoulder, neck, and forearm muscles were measured most, often alongside motion tracking or questionnaires. In the small set comparing both approaches, robot assistance consistently showed lower muscle activity, especially in the upper body, though the authors urge caution given the thin base.
plos-pone-0353058:
Abd El-Baky and colleagues, in a 2026 study, try to make an old drug, metronidazole, work better against a germ that infects the urinary tract.
