The germ, Proteus mirabilis, often strikes people with catheters and can help form stones. It also resists many drugs. The team's idea is to tuck the drug inside ring-shaped sugar carriers called cyclodextrins.

Three kinds of carrier were mixed with the drug by simple blending or kneading. Lab tests checked how the pairs formed and how fast the drug was released. Two carriers improved release, and one pairing needed a much lower dose to slow the germ. At doses too low to kill, the paired drug still cut the germ's swimming, its stone-linked enzyme action, and its ability to build biofilms, the slimy layers that shield germs. The authors say animal studies must come next before any clinical use.
plos-pone-0353958:
Lu and colleagues, in a 2026 forensic study, ask whether chemistry in the liver and kidneys can tell how a body died in seawater and how long it has been dead. Telling real drowning from a body placed in water after death is a classic hard problem. Sixty rats were assigned to seawater drowning or to being placed in seawater after death, and tissues were sampled across three days.

Thousands of small molecules in each tissue were measured, and machine learning models were trained on the patterns. Time since death dominated the chemistry, yet the models still separated the two causes of death with very high accuracy in both organs. Separate models guessed time since death within a few hours when tested on known time points, and less well on unseen ones. The authors present the approach as a promising forensic aid under controlled conditions, not yet a courtroom tool.
plos-pone-0354358:
Henkin and colleagues, in a 2026 interview study, look inside British teams that build artificial intelligence for health care. Such projects force data scientists, doctors, patients, and managers to work as one, and the social side is inseparable from the technical. Thirteen people in young research consortia described how knowledge actually moves between these camps.

People said they constantly reshaped both their tools and their message for the audience in front of them, especially clinicians and patients. Working in AI research was new to most, which itself created friction. Clinician and patient voices were wanted, but fitting them into technical workflows took effort, and AI knowledge traveled unevenly across the team. The authors take one participant's shrug as the study's spirit: much is improvised, and teams admit they are finding out as they go. Their point is that funding good teamwork is part of building good medical AI.
plos-pone-0353358:
Rodrigo Torres-Avilés and three colleagues show that a classic database question can be answered without unpacking the data, in this 2026 PLOS ONE computer science paper. A skyline query finds records that no other record beats on every measure at once — the hotels, say, that are each cheapest or best-rated in some unbeatable combination. The team implemented two flavours of the query inside a compact tree structure that stores data in compressed form.

Working directly on the compressed structure saved memory compared with ordinary approaches in their experiments, while still returning exact answers. They back the method with full proofs and benchmarks. Compact querying matters wherever data outgrow the machine that must answer questions about them.
plos-pone-0333158:
Brian Dominguez and five colleagues use songbirds to study how a Parkinson's-linked protein quiets the brain circuits for voice, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Male zebra finches sing through a dedicated brain nucleus much like the circuits that fail in human speech. The team delivered extra copies of the human alpha-synuclein gene into that nucleus, then recorded individual neurons while the birds were anaesthetised.

One class of neurons — those with broad electrical spikes — fired far less than normal after the gene treatment, with an odd rebound after each peak. Earlier work showed the same treatment makes songs softer and shorter. Connecting cell-level quieting to voice loss may help explain why Parkinson's so often steals speech early.
plos-pone-0353558:
Jiuwei Chi and seven colleagues reconstruct the carbon footprint of farming in Inner Mongolia from 2006 to 2023, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The region grows grain in dry country, leaning hard on irrigation, fertiliser, diesel, and plastic mulch. Counting the emissions embedded in those six inputs year by year, the team traced how the footprint evolved as China's farming modernised.

Input use surged early, then steadied or fell back after the mid-2010s for fertiliser, pesticide, and diesel — while plastic film kept climbing and irrigated area jumped late in the period. The pattern shows a system halfway through its low-carbon turn, with film and water now the stubborn fronts for policy.
plos-pone-0335558:
Du and colleagues built a compact vision system for spotting small objects in tennis matches in a 2026 study. The ball moves fast, players block views, and backgrounds are busy, so standard detectors often miss key items. Their system sharpens edges, weighs image channels more wisely, and punishes errors on hard small targets more strongly.

The team also labeled a new set of more than six thousand match images showing players, rackets, and balls. The system beat its base version on accuracy while staying small and fast enough for live use. Such a tool could support referees, coaches reviewing tactics, and broadcasters adding live graphics.
plos-pone-0352858:
Karahan and Kasnakoglu designed flight control for a swarm of small drones facing several troubles at once in a 2026 study. Wind, noisy sensors, and delayed messages each unsettle a flying formation, yet past work often handled them one at a time. Their framework plans paths and dodges obstacles while treating all three troubles together.

Math analysis set bounds on how far the swarm could drift from its path under limited disturbance. Computer flights in two formation shapes reached targets, kept formation, and passed fixed obstacles without crashes. Brief shape bending appeared under stress, then the swarm recovered. The unified approach suits rescue and inspection work where conditions rarely stay clean.
plos-pone-0352758:
Patricia Jurado-Gonzalez and five colleagues developed this 2026 PLOS One questionnaire for measuring how confident Spanish university students feel about cooking. Students often eat poorly after leaving home, and confidence in the kitchen is tied to better diets, yet Spain had no validated tool for this group. The team built items from existing questionnaires, had food experts review them, and piloted the draft at four Catalan universities.

After revisions, the final tool holds twenty-five items in two subscales. Student answers hung together consistently, and scores stayed stable when the questionnaire was repeated two weeks later. The authors offer it as a ready instrument for researchers and campus health programs that want to track, and eventually raise, students' cooking confidence.
plos-pone-0349858:
Fiaz Majeed and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS One study comparing machine learning models that predict the Air Quality Index for Karachi and Peshawar, two major Pakistani cities. Dirty air drives breathing illness, and forecasting its quality helps officials warn the public in time. The authors trained four regression models on recent local pollution data covering gases and fine particles.

All four models predicted the index effectively when judged by standard error measures. Careful scaling of the data before training proved important for getting the best results, and performance differed somewhat between the two cities. The authors argue that such models, fed with current local data, can give city agencies a cheap and timely forecasting tool for smog-prone regions.
plos-pone-0353158:
Maite Alanya-Pineda and six colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study linking depressive symptoms to balance problems in older adults living in twelve high Andean communities in Peru. Mountain life brings low oxygen and scarce health services, which may raise rates of both conditions. The team reanalyzed survey data collected between 2013 and 2020 from more than four hundred residents, using a short depression questionnaire and a reach test for balance.

About half the residents showed depressive symptoms, and about half had balance disorders. After adjustment, those with depressive symptoms were about two-thirds more likely to have balance trouble than those without. The authors call for larger studies and for screening programs that catch both problems early, since together they raise the risk of falls and lost independence.
plos-pone-0353258:
Niilo Liuhto and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study testing whether fragments of DNA floating in blood predict bad outcomes in advanced kidney disease. Such cell-free DNA is a newer inflammation marker never checked in patients whose kidneys are failing but who have not yet started dialysis. The team measured it in nearly one hundred forty patients and followed them for several years.

The marker predicted nothing: not deaths, heart events, emergency visits, hospital stays, or new cancers. Levels did rise later in patients who moved on to transplants or dialysis, suggesting the treatment stage itself shifts the marker. The authors present the negative result as useful guidance, sparing future studies from chasing a marker that does not deliver in this group.
plos-pone-0352658:
Bony Lestari and seven colleagues count what tuberculosis care costs patients before treatment even starts. Their 2026 study is set in Bandung, Indonesia. It focuses on drug-resistant tuberculosis, which is harder and slower to diagnose. Patients often visit several providers before anyone confirms the disease. Every visit adds fees, tests, travel, and food costs.

Interviews with two hundred fifty-eight patients reconstructed those early expenses. The typical patient had spent roughly forty-five US dollars before treatment began. Costs spread across administration, chest X-rays, laboratory tests, medicines, travel, and food. Most patients first sought help at community health centres, and many lived in rural areas. Knowing where the money leaks out helps programmes shorten the path to diagnosis and protect poor families from early financial harm.
plos-pone-0352358:
Weiping Ma proposes a new way to outline organs in three-dimensional medical scans in this 2026 paper. Drawing those outlines by hand is slow expert work. Semi-supervised learning cuts the burden by learning from a few labelled scans plus many unlabelled ones. Ma's framework sets two networks to teach each other. A cross-attention module lets them exchange detailed features as they learn.

The two branches follow a teacher-student design built on a VNet backbone. Extra losses keep their feature distributions aligned and their classes cleanly separated. Knowledge flows in both directions, so each network corrects the other. Tests used left atrium scans and pancreatic scans, two hard segmentation targets. The method outperformed existing approaches on both. Hospitals could gain accurate scan outlines while labelling only a fraction of their image archives.
plos-pone-0352158:
Lamia Jouini and six colleagues evaluate anti-stigma training for medical students in Tunisia. Their 2026 study tests a programme called READ. It teaches future doctors to respond to discrimination experienced or expected by people with mental illness. Knowledge, attitudes, and practical skills were measured before and after training. A control group allowed fair comparison, and a mock clinical exam tested real behaviour with patients.

Attitudes improved clearly in the trained group. Their stigma scores fell well beyond the control group's movement. Skills improved too. Trained students were over four times more likely to pass the practical exam. That exam grades how a student actually handles a patient describing discrimination. Knowledge and warmth on paper are not enough in a clinic room. The results encourage wider use of the training, and further research into which parts of it drive the change.
plos-pone-0352258:
Yanni Huang, Fuhua Yang, and Keli Yin surveyed eleven hundred four university students in Yunnan, China, about the good parts of their childhoods and their present happiness. Warm, safe, supportive early experiences are thought to echo into adult life. Scales measured those early experiences, the students' resilience, and their sense of well-being.

Students who recalled more positive childhood experiences reported stronger well-being as young adults. Resilience explained part of the link: good early experiences seemed to build the ability to bounce back, which in turn supported happiness. The tie was partial, so childhood warmth also matters in other ways. The authors urge colleges to train resilience while noting the sample came from one province, so the pattern needs testing in other places and cultures.
plos-pone-0351958:
Savina Chham and colleagues asked whether Cambodia's community health workers could take on a bigger role against diabetes and high blood pressure, two diseases climbing fast while clinics run short of staff. They surveyed a hundred fifty-three active workers on knowledge, attitudes, and current practice, and interviewed officials about the barriers to widening the workers' role.

The workers scored well on general questions about these diseases, risk factors, and prevention, with about nine in ten answering correctly. Gaps showed on specifics: only a fifth to two fifths knew that family history and tobacco count as risk factors. Most already did some related tasks and felt positive about the work. Money and supplies, not willingness, are the choke points, so any expanded role needs funding and kit behind it.
plos-pone-0351858:
Yitian Ou and colleagues traced how immune cells inside prostate tumors coach the cancer to spread. The cells are macrophages in their wound-healing mode. They release a growth signal called M-CSF. The team's earlier work had already flagged that signal. This study hunted the protein inside the cancer cell that answers it. They scanned the full protein output of treated prostate cancer cells.

One protein stood out: PCLAF. Checks in patient data backed its importance. Tumor tissue from seventy-nine men pointed the same way. Turning PCLAF up or down in lab tests moved invasion and migration with it. The chain now runs from an immune signal to one named effector. That gives drug hunters a narrower target in advanced disease.
plos-pone-0340658:
Karthik Kailasam and colleagues reviewed cardiac arrests inside one medical intensive care unit. Patients there are already critically ill, and many arrest under full monitoring. Survival still stays poor. The team asked which traits of the patient and the rescue effort predicted death. They adjusted for age, illness severity, and the first heart rhythm recorded.

One finding dominates the results. Every extra minute of CPR raised the odds of death. That held for death during the attempt and for death before leaving the unit. Survivors had also arrived less sick than those who died. Minutes are the currency of these events. Long rescues in failing bodies rarely end in recovery, and this study puts a number on that bedside truth.
plos-pone-0351658:
Bethany Ridley and colleagues validated new body size scales for young adults. The scales are photo-realistic figures built from three-dimensional scans of real eighteen-year-olds. Clinics and researchers need pictures that people can point to when judging body size. Older sets are often cartoon-like or built from older bodies. A hundred ten volunteers aged eighteen to twenty-five judged the figures. They estimated sizes and ranked the figures twice, three days apart.

The volunteers ranked the figures in step with the true body mass steps built into them. Their size estimates were accurate too. Scores held steady across the two sessions, with reliability from good to excellent. Young adults face high weight-related risk yet are often skipped in program design. A checked visual ruler for this age band fills a real gap.
plos-pone-0351758:
Aishwa Roy and Protima Sarker tested bone meal powder, ground animal bone, as a homegrown phosphorus fertilizer for Malabar spinach. Chemical phosphorus fertilizer is pricey and polluting, and mined phosphate is finite, so alternatives matter. They ran the powder in two soils, one salty and one not, tracking soil chemistry, then grew spinach in pots to watch germination and early growth.

The bone meal raised soil pH and clearly lifted the phosphorus plants could reach in both soils. The plant side was mixed: germination and some early growth measures suffered in the non-salty soil even as shoots lengthened, while roots and fresh weight changed little. The authors call it promising but unfinished business, asking for field trials before farmers swap their fertilizer bags for bone meal.
plos-pone-0343158:
Shiming Wang and colleagues propose a data-driven system for keeping the cost of building commercial complexes, malls and mixed-use giants, under control. Such projects sprawl across functions and trades, and overruns hide until late. Their framework applies value engineering, a discipline that prices every function a building must perform, and ranks those functions with a fuzzy version of a standard priority method that tolerates expert disagreement.

Cost and value coefficients for each function are then watched in real time, flagging construction choices whose price outruns their worth while change is still cheap. The authors validated the approach by re-running an existing complex through it and comparing the outcome with what actually happened. For developers, the appeal is a control room for cost that argues in functions, not just invoices.
plos-pone-0351158:
Online shops increasingly let buyers try products virtually, draping clothes or placing furniture through augmented reality. Xiaodong Zhang and colleagues surveyed about four hundred eighty shoppers to learn how such features shape the wish to buy, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Four features were tested: virtual try-on, hands-on product displays, blending virtual goods into real rooms, and personal suggestions. Each raised buying intention indirectly, by lifting how valuable the shopping felt and how warmly people viewed the brand. None acted straight through. The authors advise sellers to design reality tools around felt value and brand feeling, not novelty alone.
plos-pone-0350858:
Kazuya Hosokawa and colleagues set out a study plan, with no results yet, for spotting a treatable cause of high pressure in the lungs. Blocked lung arteries after clots can raise that pressure, yet diagnosis often comes late and the best scan is scarce outside large centres. A moving chest X ray method can map blood flow in the lungs quickly.

Readers will judge real cases in random order, some with standard tests alone and some with the moving X ray added. Final diagnoses follow Japanese and European rules. The team will compare accuracy, hits, and misses, and check how well the new method matches the scarce scan. If it works, more hospitals could screen without delay.
plos-pone-0351058:
Ziqiao Ding and colleagues argue that supply chains need embodied intelligence, where sensing, thinking, and physical action join in one loop. Most research tunes algorithms on data alone, leaving a gap between digital plans and real warehouses and trucks. Their framework stacks four layers: sensing the world, reasoning in context, acting physically, and feeding results back for learning.

Fragmented sensing and slow feedback are named as core faults in current chains. By naming those faults and mapping how each layer should inform the next, the paper sets an agenda for theory, tools, and practice. Chains that learn from physical outcomes, the authors claim, will adapt faster than chains that only replan on screens.
plos-pone-0350658:
Yiwen Wei, Lingxiao Guo, and Qunshan Tao studied how China's carbon cutting and public health services develop together across provinces from 2012 to 2023, in work published in 2026. National goals push both agendas at once, and whether they advance in step was unknown.

The team scored carbon governance and health service efficiency for thirty-one provinces, then measured how tightly the two were coupled and where gaps concentrate. National coupling wobbled early, then rose steadily. Regional inequality and clustering patterns were mapped, and factors behind them tested. The results help provinces see whether green and health progress reinforce or crowd each other.
plos-pone-0349558:
Jinmeng Bi, Ye Li, and Yuhang Pan mapped earthquake patterns across North China using records from 1970 to 2025 in work published in 2026. The region is one of continental China's most active, and two pattern measures may reveal stress building before big shocks.

After removing aftershock clusters statistically, the team measured how spread out quakes are in space and the balance of small to large events. Removing clusters raised the spread measure. High spread sat in fractured zones, low in the stable Ordos block. Spread fell before main shocks and recovered after, a rhythm that could one day aid watchfulness, though not prediction.
plos-pone-0349758:
Blanca Lumbreras and colleagues surveyed Spanish doctors about prostate cancer screening with the PSA blood test. Newer European guidance favors risk-based screening and shared decisions with patients, rather than testing everyone. General practitioners and urologists both order these tests, so the study compared the two groups' knowledge, attitudes, and habits across nearly five hundred respondents.

The questionnaire was built through an expert consensus process and covered opinions, daily practice, and guideline knowledge. Differences between the specialties matter because a man's path to diagnosis usually starts with whichever doctor he sees first. Where the two groups disagree on testing or on involving patients in the choice, screening practice will vary for reasons that have nothing to do with the patient.
plos-pone-0348058:
Shruti Khanduri and co-workers lay out a trial plan testing Trikatu, a classic Ayurvedic spice blend, as an add-on for people with unhealthy blood fats. Many patients in poorer countries stop cholesterol drugs early, so a culturally familiar helper could matter. Their 2026 protocol describes a blinded trial at a major Indian hospital with one hundred seventy adults at raised heart risk.

Half will take Trikatu twice a day for twelve weeks alongside their usual statin, and half a matching dummy pill. Blood fats form the main measure, with sugar, swelling markers, blood pressure, and gut microbes also tracked. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet; it tests whether tradition and modern care can be judged fairly together.
plos-pone-0348758:
Enjing Xiao and co-workers improve a camera-based defect spotter for the banded edges of wooden furniture panels. Edge banding flaws are small and easy to miss, which costs makers rework and returns. Their 2026 study upgrades a compact detection model with feature blending across scales, a sharper pooling block with attention, and a loss rule that settles faster on the flaw's true box.

On a purpose-built photo set of panel edges, the improved model scored higher on the standard detection measure than the base model it grew from. The authors describe fewer misses and fewer false alarms as the practical payoff. Automated edge checks could steady quality on furniture lines where tired eyes now do the watching.
plos-pone-0347758:
He-Ping Liu and colleagues tested an extract from Syzygium brachythyrsum, a plant long used by the Dai people of Yunnan, China, against artery clogging in mice. The extract is rich in polyphenols, plant chemicals with antioxidant effects. Mice bred to develop atherosclerosis ate a high-fat diet for twelve weeks, with some receiving the extract and others a standard cholesterol drug.

Treated mice developed smaller fatty plaques in the aorta and stored less fat in the liver, with calmer inflammation and less oxidative damage. Cell experiments traced the benefit to a protective antioxidant pathway, and blocking that pathway erased the effect. The authors suggest the extract merits study as a companion therapy for heart disease.
plos-pone-0336358:
Ao Qiao, Siyu Zeng, and Jianing Wang model what happens when two climate policies run at once, in this 2026 PLOS ONE economics paper. Governments increasingly pair cap-and-trade, which limits total emissions, with subsidies for low-carbon production, yet most research studies each policy alone and ignores factory-floor details such as batch sizes.

The authors set up a game between a manufacturer and a retailer, with the factory's production queue modeled to capture real emissions, and test different policy mixes. Comparing the outcomes shows how the two policies can reinforce or undercut each other, and what contract terms keep the supply chain cooperating. The results are meant for policy makers designing combined carbon rules.
plos-pone-0347858:
Mohammad Kazemi, Reza Naderi Samani, and Narges Kariminejad build a flood-risk map for Khuzestan Province in Iran in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Flood mapping depends heavily on which landscape factors the model uses and how it is tuned, so the team combined satellite data from Google Earth Engine with a careful selection process.

Nineteen candidate factors were scored by nine different selection methods, and the most consistently chosen fed a deep learning network whose settings were tuned by an optimization algorithm. One thousand sampled points, half flooded and half not, trained the model before it was applied across the province. Planners could use such maps to steer building and defenses away from the likeliest flood paths.
plos-pone-0348358:
Hessam Noori-Dokht and colleagues examine a hidden source of noise in cartilage injury experiments, in this 2026 PLOS ONE biomechanics paper. Labs study joint injury by striking a rabbit's knee cartilage with a controlled impact, but the joint is pinned by a metal wire whose exact placement varies from specimen to specimen.

Measuring impacts on cadaver knees, the team found that where the wire sat front-to-back strongly predicted peak stress, loading speed, impact duration, and total work, while its up-down position mattered little. Bone failure measures shifted with placement too. Standardizing wire position, they argue, would make injury models more repeatable, so treatments tested in animals rest on cleaner comparisons.
plos-pone-0347958:
Laila Farouk and colleagues chart drug resistance in urinary infections in Tétouan, Morocco. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Urinary infections rank among the most common bacterial illnesses. Gut-related bacteria cause most of them. Three labs in the city gathered isolates from outpatients in 2022 and 2023. The set held more than four hundred isolates.

Each isolate was named by machine and tested against key drugs. Extra checks hunted for enzymes that defeat whole drug families. Doctors treat these infections before test results come back. So a local map of what still works guides first choices. Outdated guesses breed resistance instead. The study gives Moroccan clinics that map.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Cyprus was being torn apart in the summer of 1974. After a coup backed by Greece, Turkey had invaded, and fighting continued despite repeated Council demands to stop. Resolution 358, adopted unanimously on 15 August 1974, came one day after an earlier ceasefire order had been ignored, a failure the text openly deplores.

The members recalled their chain of Cyprus resolutions from July and August 1974 and insisted that all parties carry them out in full. Above all, they demanded immediate and strict respect for the ceasefire. The resolution is short, but its tone shows a Council losing patience with orders that were not being obeyed.

Senegal's path to this text ran through a failed federation. It had shared the short-lived Mali Federation with its neighbor. That union broke apart in August 1960. Senegal then applied for its own UN seat. Resolution 158 was adopted unanimously on 28 September 1960 at the 907th meeting.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Senegal. Admission came the same day in the Assembly, a rare same-day double. Senegal joined during the celebrated Year of Africa. Its first president, Léopold Senghor, became a leading voice of the new African bloc. The one-sentence resolution marks Senegal's formal entry onto the world stage.

Guns kept seeping into Somalia in 2004, twelve years into a ban. A UN watch team had just sent its first report, dated 11 August. Its finds were grim. Talks to rebuild a Somali state ran in parallel. Resolution 1558 passed with no dissent on 17 August 2004.

The watch team was brought back for six months. The chief had thirty days to set it up. Its chores were clear. Track the flow of arms in and out of Somalia. Keep a fresh list of ban-breakers and their backers. Send the sanctions group a mid-term and a last word. All states were told the ban still bound them in full. The team was urged to hone its list with care, for steps the Council might take later.

Liberia's file came back for a short, sharp look in 2003. A team of sleuths had probed the state's rule the past fall. Their word came on 25 October 2002. The charge was plain: did Monrovia obey the bans laid on it in 2001? War in next-door Côte d'Ivoire made the file burn hot. Resolution 1458 passed with no dissent on 28 January 2003.

The sleuth team was brought back for three months. It would start by 10 February at the late. Five sleuths at most would do the work. They would tour Liberia and the states round it. Old audits of state cash would get a fresh read. Rebel moves fell in their scope too. Their word was due by 16 April 2003. A full six-month check on the bans loomed in May.

Resolution 58, adopted on 28 September 1948, sorts out how Switzerland can help choose World Court judges without joining the UN. Switzerland had met the Assembly's conditions and become a party to the court's statute, even accepting the court's compulsory jurisdiction. Elections for the court were coming at the next Assembly session, and the statute required the Council to recommend the terms for such states.

The Council recommended that a state in Switzerland's position stand on an equal footing with UN members in nominating candidates. It would vote in the Assembly on the same terms as members. One limit applied: a state behind on its payments toward the court's expenses could not take part in electing judges.

Resolution 1958, passed on 15 December 2010, shuts down the last gears of Iraq's oil-for-food scheme. The scheme, born in 1995, was a stopgap under the bans on Iraq. It let Iraq sell oil to buy food and drugs for its people. It shut in form in 2003. Yet stray tasks dragged on for years: old credit notes with claims still live, as a UN note of that December set out in depth.

The Council told the UN chief to take all steps to end the scheme's last tasks for good. It noted that the stray credit notes had lapsed by their own terms. Two twin Iraq texts passed the same day. With them, the books closed on a huge relief plan, one later stained by fraud probes.

A stalled settlement process shadows Resolution 1758 on Cyprus, adopted on 15 June 2007. The island stayed generally calm, though buffer-zone violations had risen. The 8 July 2006 Agreement, aiming at a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality, still had not been put into effect. Demining in the buffer zone had stalled, and housing for many UNFICYP troops was poor.

The Council extends the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 15 December 2007. It says the status quo is unacceptable and time is not on the side of a settlement. It calls on both sides to engage at once, show measurable progress, and stop trading blame so full negotiations can begin. It asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. Talks on the buffer zone, including the Ledra Street crossing, are urged. A report is due by 1 December 2007.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2758 (XXVI), adopted on 25 October 1971, settled who speaks for China at the United Nations. The Assembly held that restoring the lawful rights of the People's Republic of China was vital. It was vital to guard the Charter and the cause the United Nations serves. It held that its government's delegates were China's only lawful voice.

The decision restored all rights to the People's Republic of China. It named it one of the five permanent members of the Security Council. It ordered the prompt removal of the delegates who had held China's seat until then. They were to be removed from the United Nations and all bodies tied to it.

General Assembly resolution 69/58 (2014) follows up its high-level meeting on nuclear disarmament, held on 26 September 2013. It backs the wide support voiced there for a comprehensive convention on nuclear weapons. It calls for negotiations to begin in the Conference on Disarmament. The negotiations are on a convention banning the weapons and providing for their destruction. It recalls the decision to hold a United Nations conference on nuclear disarmament by 2018. It welcomes the naming of 26 September as the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Behind closed doors on 27 June 2001, the Council took up one short question: who should lead the United Nations next. Having considered the matter, it recommended to the General Assembly that Kofi Annan be appointed Secretary-General for a second term, running from 1 January 2002 to 31 December 2006. Under the Charter, the Council's recommendation comes first and the Assembly then makes the appointment, so this brief text is the formal step that set the second term in motion.

Haiti had just held the first round of its elections on 7 February 2006, and on 14 February its stabilization mission, MINUSTAH, is extended until 15 August 2006. Haitians are congratulated on the successful vote. Municipal and local elections were still to come in April.

All Haitians are urged to keep taking part in the political process and accept its results peacefully. The mission's central role in supporting the remaining elections and Haiti's longer recovery is restated. The Secretary-General is asked to report soon on the situation, including how the mission should be shaped for the period after the new elected president took office.

Burundi's integrated office, BINUB, is extended until 31 December 2009 on 22 December 2008. Heads of state of the Great Lakes region had met in Bujumbura on 4 December and agreed steps with the Palipehutu-FNL, the last rebel movement. Carrying out the 2006 ceasefire with that group was the main unfinished piece of Burundi's peace.

The government and the FNL are urged to carry out their December agreements before the end of 2008 and to settle the rest by dialogue, without any return to fighting. The FNL is called on to release child soldiers and join the disarmament process. BINUB would keep supporting peace consolidation, justice, and security reform while the final phase of the peace process closed.

The situation in the Middle East kept getting worse after the 1967 war, and the Council spoke on 18 September 1968. Resolution 258 insisted that the cease-fire the Council had ordered must be strictly respected. It reaffirmed Resolution 242 of 1967, the landmark text on settling the conflict. That text called for Israeli withdrawal from occupied territories and for all states in the area to live in peace. All parties were urged to cooperate fully with the Secretary-General's special envoy, who was working to carry out that plan.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed once more on 14 December 1979, by Resolution 458. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 1 December, recommended six more months. The parties concerned agreed with the recommendation. Cyprus accepted that the force should stay beyond 15 December.

The Council extended the force's stationing to 15 June 1980. It voiced support for a ten-point agreement meant to restart the talks between the two communities. That agreement had been worked out at a high-level meeting in Nicosia in May 1979. The parties were urged to resume the talks without delay. The talks had to be steady and focused on results. The Secretary-General was to continue his mission of good offices and report by 31 May 1980.
un-sc-res-358:
Cyprus's ceasefire was breaking down within weeks of the 1974 fighting. On 15 August 1974 the Security Council deplored the failure to obey its order of the day before. Resolution 357 had demanded that the shooting stop. Violence and bloodshed on the island went on. The Council's patience in the text is plainly thin. It had already passed four Cyprus resolutions in under a month.

The Council insists on full use of all those resolutions. Every party had to follow them. The ceasefire had to be observed at once and strictly. The demand covered resolutions 353, 354, 355, and 357. Together they called for a halt, talks, and respect for Cyprus's sovereignty.
un-sc-res-1558:
Somalia's arms embargo needed fresh watchers in the summer of 2004. A monitoring group had reported that month on breaches of the ban. On 17 August 2004 the Security Council ordered the group rebuilt. The Secretary-General had thirty days to re-establish it. It would work for a further period with a fresh mandate. The 1992 embargo remained in force, and all states had to honor it.

The Council said it would study the group's findings with care. Better enforcement of the embargo was the goal. The Secretary-General also had to arrange the money for the work. Somalia's reconciliation process ran in parallel in Kenya. The monitors' reports fed the sanctions committee named for resolution 751.
un-sc-res-1458:
Liberia's sanctions panel was sent back to work in January 2003. The Council's next review of the Liberia measures was due by May. Fighting in Liberia and nearby Côte d'Ivoire caused deep concern. On 28 January 2003 the Council took note of the panel's October report. It said it would keep giving that report full attention. The panel had tracked how Liberia's government met the Council's demands.

The panel was re-established for three more months. Its new term had to start by 10 February 2003. It would run a follow-up mission to Liberia and nearby states. The mission would check compliance with the demands in resolution 1343. Those demands covered Liberia's support for rebels abroad. The panel's findings would guide the May review.
un-sc-res-58:
Switzerland's path into the World Court's elections was set by the Security Council on 28 September 1948. Switzerland had joined the Statute of the International Court of Justice under conditions the General Assembly laid down in December 1946. It had even accepted the Court's compulsory jurisdiction. With judge elections due, the Council had to recommend terms for states in Switzerland's position.

The Council recommended that a state party to the Statute but not a United Nations member stand equal with members in nominating candidates. Such a state would vote in the General Assembly for judges in the same manner as members. One bar applied: a state behind on its payments to the Court's expenses, by two full years or more, could not vote. The Assembly could excuse arrears caused by events beyond the state's control. The formula let Switzerland and later others join the Court's system without membership.
un-sc-res-1758:
Cyprus and its long division return in Resolution 1758 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 15 June 2007. The island stayed broadly calm, yet buffer zone violations had risen. A deal reached on 8 July 2006 still waited for action, and mine clearing had stalled.

The text extends the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, called UNFICYP, until 15 December 2007. It calls the frozen state of affairs flatly unacceptable. Both leaders are urged to start the agreed process at once and show real progress. The Council also asks the Turkish Cypriot side to let mine clearing resume in the buffer zone.
un-ga-res-china-s-position-paper-on-the-:
China's seat at the United Nations changed hands through General Assembly resolution 2758 in October 1971, and this position paper states Beijing's view of that vote. Before 1971 the seat was held by the government on Taiwan. The resolution gave the seat to the People's Republic of China instead.

The paper argues that the vote settled the question of who speaks for China. It backs the one-China line and rejects any claim of two Chinas or a separate Taiwan seat. The text matters because the 1971 vote is still cited in fights over Taiwan's status today.
europmc-pmc10007858:
Yuan and co-workers review how the matrix around a tumor changes as cancer grows and learns to hide from the immune system, in a 2023 paper. A tumor is not just cancer cells. It sits in a scaffold of proteins and support cells that it reshapes to feed its own spread.

The authors trace how that reshaping helps tumors grow and escape immune attack. They then survey treatments that target the scaffold itself. The review connects basic cell science to drug ideas now in testing, in terms a general reader can follow.
europmc-pmc10390758:
Chen and co-authors gave a 2023 guide to multi-omics, a way to study disease with many data types at once. Each omics layer reads one part of the cell, such as genes, RNA, proteins, or small chemicals. Joining the layers can show how a disease works as a whole system. The guide is aimed at newcomers to the field.

Chen lays out the main tech types and warns on how to design a sound study. Machine learning and deep learning help merge the layers into one picture. Uses span cancer, brain disease, ageing, and the hunt for drug targets. Newer forms read single cells or keep each cell's place in tissue. The guide lists free tools and data banks for the work.
europmc-pmc10393958:
Choi and Park reviewed a stress protein called TXNIP in 2023 and its role in disease. TXNIP binds a guard protein, thioredoxin, that shields cells from damage. By gripping that guard, TXNIP weakens the shield and raises cell stress. New work shows the protein does far more than that.

Choi reports that TXNIP can switch on a danger complex that sparks swelling inside cells. It can also push cells toward death under stress from their inner stores. These acts link TXNIP to diabetes, kidney disease, and brain disorders. Drugs that block TXNIP are thus of keen interest. The review weighs how such drugs might treat these diseases.
europmc-pmc10497558:
Ling and co-authors reviewed amino acid metabolism in health and disease in 2023. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Cells also burn them for energy and use them to grow and split. When their handling goes wrong, illness can follow across many organs.

Tumours lean hard on amino acids taken in from food and blood. Ling reports that blocking select paths can starve tumour cells while sparing normal ones. Immune cells also hinge on these paths, from killer T cells to calming Treg cells. The review spans cancer first, then metabolic, heart, and immune diseases. Each path offers fresh points where a drug might act.
europmc-pmc11256658:
Zheng and colleagues report national cancer statistics for China in 2016 in this 2022 paper. China's National Cancer Center publishes such figures yearly from population registries. For 2016, a total of 487 registries supplied high-quality data on new cases and deaths. Nationwide totals were estimated by scaling registry data to the national population.

China saw about 4.06 million new cancer cases in 2016, and about 2.41 million cancer deaths, they estimate. Lung, colorectal, stomach, liver, and female breast cancers were the five most common, at 57.4 percent of new cases. Lung, liver, stomach, colorectal, and oesophageal cancers led deaths, at 69.3 percent of the total. Rates were split by urban and rural area, sex, and fine age groups. Age-standardised rates used the world Segi population as the reference.
europmc-pmc11298558:
He, Zhou, and Wang review glycosylation, a sugar-tagging of proteins, in this 2024 paper. After a protein is built, cells often modify it by adding or removing chemical groups. Glycosylation transfers sugar chains onto specific amino acid sites using enzymes called glycosyltransferases. It ranks among the most common such modifications.

The tagging is essential for protein function, cell adhesion, and immune escape, the authors note. Faulty patterns are closely linked to cancer, inflammation, and autoimmune disorders. Yet the exact composition and structure of the sugar tags remain undetermined in many cases. The review argues for deeper mapping of tag structures and their varying levels across tissues. It also urges pairing that mapping with advanced detection technologies. Clinical implications run through the paper's closing sections.
europmc-pmc1175958:
Smith and colleagues propose strict definitions for the relations used in biomedical ontologies in this 2005 paper. An ontology is a controlled vocabulary: a fixed list of terms for a field, with definitions. Many biomedical lists use relations such as part-of and located-in loosely. The paper is part of a reform effort by the Open Biomedical Ontologies group.

The authors advance a method for giving each relational term a consistent, unambiguous formal definition. The goal is to help developers and users avoid errors in coding and annotation. The Gene Ontology shows the stakes: it holds three vocabularies, for cell components, molecular function, and biological process, and is reused by databases worldwide. A sloppy relation, copied everywhere, spreads silent errors. The method is offered for ontology building across the life sciences.
europmc-pmc1241758:
O'Neill and a workshop group tackled how wealth shapes pollution harm in 2003. Air pollution and social position each affect health on their own. Poor and working-class areas often face higher pollution too. Early studies hinted social position changes pollution effects themselves.

The authors propose theories for how the two forces interact. They draw on studies from around the world. Methods from air pollution science and social epidemiology are introduced side by side. Gaps in study design get direct attention. O'Neill calls for joint research that treats exposure and inequality together.
europmc-pmc1274258:
Larionov, Krause, and Miller described a standard-curve method for PCR data in 2005. Real-time PCR is the most precise way to measure gene activity. Raw output is a mass of glow numbers. Processing choices can shift final results a lot.

Their procedure skips efficiency estimation entirely. Noise is filtered by smoothing, baseline removal, and scaling. The reading threshold is picked on its own from the standard curve. Crossing points come straight from curve coordinates. Variation within each run gets a statistical estimate. Larionov cuts operator handling to a minimum. It appeared in BMC Bioinformatics in 2005. It ran in BMC Bioinformatics in 2005.
europmc-pmc1403158:
Ocean water teems with archaea, microbes akin to bacteria but with their own branch of life. Hallam and co-authors read genes from one such microbe in 2006, a sea form that lives with a sponge host. They rebuilt its likely routes for taking in carbon and gaining energy from those gene clues.

The genes point to a changed three-step cycle that fixes carbon dioxide into food. Other genes suggest the microbe can also eat organic carbon. Hallam also found genes for using ammonia as fuel. Matching genes turned up in seas worldwide. The work hints these tiny microbes help run ocean carbon and nitrogen cycles.
europmc-pmc1601958:
Drug hunters need to know where a drug can lodge on a protein. Huang and Schroeder improved a site-finding algorithm in 2006, LIGSITEcsc. It scans a protein surface for pockets, using geometry based on the Connolly surface, a smooth skin over the molecule.

The upgrade re-ranks candidate pockets by how conserved their surface residues are across species. Conserved spots tend to matter, so ranking by them greatly improved accuracy. On 48 paired and 210 bound structures, the tool hit success rates of 71 and 75 percent. Huang offers a web server and free source code.
europmc-pmc1634758:
Repetitive DNA clutters every complex genome, and curating it needs tools. Kohany and co-authors presented two in 2006 for Repbase, the reference database of repeats. RepbaseSubmitter formats and annotates new entries through a Java interface.

It auto-computes sequence length and composition, cutting common formatting errors. It can also predict protein-coding regions and pull in PubMed references and species data. The second tool, Censor, scans a new sequence against known repeats at speed. Its output maps the repeats found and can mask them. Both tools run as web services or downloads, Kohany reports.
europmc-pmc1635058:
Putting research into practice in veterans' hospitals needs more than memos. Stetler and co-authors evaluated external facilitation in 2006 within QUERI, a quality program of the Veterans Health Administration. Facilitators are helpers sent from outside a site to ease change.

Through interviews across several multi-site projects, the team found facilitation to be a deliberate, valued process. It joined interactive problem solving with support, tailored to each site's snags. Facilitators differed from other change agents by working problems live with local teams. Stetler argues the role deserves a clear definition, since studies had used the term loosely.
europmc-pmc1635558:
Back pain scales abound, but which detects change best? Lauridsen and co-authors compared five instruments head to head in 2006, in 191 Danish patients from primary and hospital care. They included two disability surveys, parts of a general health survey, a back pain rating scale, and a simple pain number scale.

The Roland Morris questionnaire was most responsive in patients with back pain only. In leg pain patients, it tied with the Oswestry index. Among patients who improved, the Roland Morris again led for back-only cases. Lauridsen gives clinics subpopulation-specific guidance instead of one verdict for all.
europmc-pmc1638158:
Children meet contaminants through air, skin, and mouth, and their habits set the dose. Cohen Hubal and co-authors reviewed in 2000 what is known about children's exposure and what data are missing. Regulators lean on default assumptions because child-specific data are scarce.

Assessing exposure needs activity patterns: where children play, what they touch, what they swallow. Such data are thinnest for the youngest children. The team calls for better age groupings for assessments, better monitoring methods, and data on contaminant levels and transfer rates. Cohen Hubal argues these gaps must close before rules can be trusted to protect children.
europmc-pmc1781458: Collagen reorganization at the tumor-stromal interface facilitates local invasion. — a 2005 science paper on collagen reshaping at tumor edges. It shows the reshaping aids spread for labs. The paper is the collagen study: the notes on tumor spread, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1885958: Initial events in establishing vaginal entry and infection by human immunodeficiency virus type-1. — a 2005 science paper on HIV vaginal entry. It studies the initial events. The paper is the entry study: the findings on HIV infection, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2186358: DAVID Knowledgebase: a gene-centered database integrating heterogeneous gene annotation resources to facilitate high-throughput gene functional analysis. — a 2005 science paper on the DAVID gene hub. It guides the DAVID gene hub for labs. The paper is the hub guide: the notes on gene tools, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2211558: CONSORT for reporting randomized controlled trials in journal and conference abstracts: explanation and elaboration. — a 2005 science paper on CONSORT abstract rules. It explains the CONSORT rules. The paper is the CONSORT guide: the findings on reporting rules, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2216058: Contributions of inflammatory processes to the development of the early stages of diabetic retinopathy. — a 2005 science paper on swelling in diabetic eye ills. It finds the swelling's role for labs. The paper is the eye-ill study: the notes on diabetic ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2561058: Accuracy of predicting the genetic risk of disease using a genome-wide approach. — a 2008 science paper on genome-wide risk prediction. It predicts the genetic risk. The paper is the risk study: the findings on disease ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2648658: Effects of climate change on ticks and tick-borne diseases in europe. — a 2008 science paper on ticks and climate change. It studies the tick-borne effects. The paper is the tick study: the findings on climate ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2654758: Bacterial toxin-antitoxin systems: more than selfish entities? — a 2008 science paper on toxin-antitoxin systems. It asks if they're more than selfish. The paper is the toxin study: the findings on bacterial ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2654858: The HELLP syndrome: clinical issues and management. A Review. — a 2008 science paper on HELLP syndrome. It reviews the clinical management. The paper is the HELLP review: the findings on syndrome ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2694358: Identifying relationships among genomic disease regions: predicting genes at pathogenic SNP ass — a 2008 science paper on disease-region genes. It identifies the genomic relationships. The paper is the gene study: the findings on disease ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2732458: Public health assessment of potential biological terrorism agents. — a 2008 science paper on bioweapon scare lists. It ranks the scare lists for labs. The paper is the rank study: the notes on scare ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2779358: Survey of the quality of experimental design, statistical analysis and reporting of research us — a 2008 science paper on research quality surveys. It surveys the experimental design. The paper is the survey study: the findings on quality ills, filed here in session.
olaus-magnus-compendious-history-streate:
Olaus Magnus, a Swedish churchman, published his great history of the northern peoples in Latin in 1555. This English version of 1658 shortens that vast work for London readers. It describes the Goths, Swedes, and Vandals, and the cold lands they came from.

Early modern Scandinavia appears here as a land of marvels. Sea serpents coil in northern waters, and mermen rise from the deep. Snow, ice, and the midnight sun shape every custom he reports. English readers of 1658 met the north mainly through such wonders. The book mixes real report with sailors' tales, and both halves are worth reading.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib4-1558:
Gesner went down into the waters for the fourth volume of his Historiae animalium in 1558. It treats fishes and water creatures of every kind, the largest survey of sea life yet attempted in print. Rivers, lakes, and oceans all contribute their tenants to his catalogue.

Whales, sharks, and common food fish receive the same careful order. Among them stand the sea serpent and other marine monsters that sailors swore were true. Gesner weighs the reports as best his age allowed. The volume keeps one foot in marvel, and is the more fascinating for it. No earlier book had tried to hold the whole watery world at once.
hocus-pocus-junior-1658:
Hocus Pocus Junior calls itself the anatomy of legerdemain, the art of sleight of hand. First printed in 1634, it appears here in its fifth edition of 1658. It is the first English book of conjuring tricks, and it gave the world the phrase hocus pocus, taken from the patter of stage jugglers.

The book explains cups and balls, card tricks, and feats with string and coin. Its aim is exposure as much as teaching: readers learn how the wonders are done. That honesty made it a landmark in the history of stage magic. Generations of conjurers learned their first tricks from its pages. A working manual and a small delight, it still performs its tricks on readers.
plos-pone-0004958:
Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare, aggressive skin cancer. Under the microscope it looks almost identical to small cell lung cancer. A new virus, Merkel cell polyomavirus, had just been found in these tumors. Charlotte Wetzels and co-authors searched for it directly. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used ultrastructural imaging of tumor cells.

The imaging gave direct proof of polyomavirus in the skin tumor cells. The same search found none in small cell lung carcinoma. That contrast marks the look-alike cancers as different diseases. The distinction matters for diagnosis and for treatment choices.
plos-pone-0005058:
Noroviruses cause epidemic stomach illness worldwide. They latch onto human blood-group sugars to infect us. Ming Tan and colleagues studied those gripping surfaces in PLOS ONE in 2009. They compared carbohydrate-binding interfaces across virus strains. Noroviruses are diverse, with two major genogroups and about thirty genotypes.

Despite that diversity, the sugar-binding interface stayed conserved. Human histo-blood group antigens shaped that conservation. Our blood types steered the virus's evolution. A conserved grip is an attractive vaccine target. It is one of the few stable features on a changing virus. The work shows host biology leaving fingerprints on a pathogen's design.
plos-pone-0005158:
TB ranges from silent infection to severe disease. Doctors need markers that tell which patients are in trouble. Zahra Hasan and colleagues measured immune responses in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used ESAT6, a protein secreted by the TB bacterium. Patient T cells respond to it with interferon-gamma. Another signal, CXCL9, was also measured.

The ESAT6-induced responses differentiated severity of tuberculosis. Interferon-gamma and CXCL9 levels separated severe from milder cases. The immune readouts act as severity gauges. They could guide who needs the most urgent care. Defense against TB depends on proper T cell and macrophage activation. This study turns that activation into a measurable signal. Triage in crowded clinics could benefit.
plos-pone-0005258:
Eating fish is linked to better health, but the steps behind the benefit are not fully known. Lankinen and colleagues used lipidomics, a full profile of blood fats, in PLOS ONE in 2009 to see what fatty fish intake changes.

Fatty fish lowered blood lipids tied to inflammation and to insulin signaling. The profile shift gives a concrete mechanism for part of the fish effect. It also hints at blood fat markers that diet studies can use to check whether advice is working. Blood fat maps of this kind could also test which fish, and how much of it, gives the best gain for the heart and for blood sugar.
plos-pone-0005358:
In multipassage experiments, human tumor cells are grown in one mouse, then moved to the next, again and again. The growth curves from those passages hold patterns about tumor behavior. Gliozzi and colleagues built a computational tool to analyze them in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their tool treats the curves phenomenologically, modeling their shape without assuming one mechanism. Fitted shapes can reveal growth laws that raw plots hide. Better curve analysis helps researchers compare tumor lines and judge how treatments change growth across passages. Mouse-passage tumors are a long-used way to test how cancer grows when it is moved again. Again, much as a tumor spreads in a body over the course of a long illness.
plos-pone-0005958:
Drug-resistant gut bacteria no longer stay inside hospitals. Jonas Bonnedahl, Mirva Drobni, Michel Gauthier-Clerc and colleagues followed one resistant strain of E. coli in the south of France in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tracks bacteria carrying CTX-M enzymes, which break down key antibiotics, in both people and yellow-legged gulls.

Finding the same resistant bacteria in gulls and in humans suggests the germs move between the two. Birds that feed near towns can carry resistance far and wide. The study adds wildlife to the map of how superbugs spread, a point that matters for doctors, vets and anyone who plans how to slow resistance.
plos-pone-0006058:
Gene delivery rides on fat bubbles that carry DNA into cells. Sarah Resina, Paul Prevot and Alain Thierry asked in 2009 what makes those bubbles work. Their PLOS ONE paper studies lipoplexes, mixes of DNA and charged lipids, including a house formula called Neutraplex that can be made with a positive, neutral or negative charge.

The bubbles' physical and chemical traits steer how cells take them in and how well the gene transfer works, the title reports. A recipe's charge and makeup are thus design choices, not details. The work helps gene therapy and lab transfection alike, since the same delivery problem sits at the heart of both.
plos-pone-0006158:
When the liver's main antioxidant system fails for good, the cell must find another guard or die. Elena Suvorova, Olivier Lucas, Carla Weisend and colleagues found the backup in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies hepatocytes chronically lacking Txnrd1, a core part of the thioredoxin system that keeps proteins reduced and feeds other antioxidant enzymes.

The protective Nrf2 pathway switches on in those cells, the title reports, compensating for the chronic loss. A standing backup explains why some knockouts look healthier than expected. The result also cautions drug work aimed at antioxidant enzymes: the cell's second line may blunt a drug meant to starve a tumor of its defenses.
plos-pone-0006258:
Ocean life is shrinking under fishing pressure, and reserves usually ban fishing in chosen spots. Natalie Ban and Amanda Vincent flip that logic in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Instead of selecting areas where fishing is prohibited, they explore selecting the areas where fishing is permitted.

The rest of the ocean then becomes protected by default. Starting from permission rather than prohibition can soften impacts on fishers and their communities. It also forces planners to justify exactly where extraction should happen. The paper offers a fresh frame for balancing marine protection with livelihoods.
plos-pone-0006658:
Hidekazu Kuwayama and Yuzuru Kubohara studied signal molecules in a slime mold in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early in the life of Dictyostelium discoideum, single cells crawl toward cAMP, a signal that draws them together. That chemotaxis builds a joined structure from lone cells. Two factors called DIF-1 and DIF-2 were known to guide which cell fate each cell takes as the structure forms.

Their title says these factors also act as modulators of chemotaxis in this slime mold. One signal can thus steer both movement and fate in the same cells. Dictyostelium is a classic model for how lone cells join into one organism. Dual-use signals are a neat, spare design worth study.
plos-pone-0006758:
Sang Ok Song and Jeffrey Varner built a mathematical model of pain signaling in sensory neurons in PLOS ONE in 2009. Calcium levels inside a cell help carry pain signals. Outside signals can raise or lower that calcium. ATP, released between cells, acts on P2 receptors to modulate calcium. The authors wanted a mechanistic account of these interactions.

Their model links ATP receptor activity to calcium dynamics step by step. A mechanistic model predicts how changes propagate through the system. It can test drug ideas before any laboratory experiment. It also shows which steps matter most for pain transmission. Such models help pain research move from description toward engineering.
plos-pone-0006858:
Kristiina Kanerva and her team studied a brake protein in mast cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mast cells are the cells that drive sneezes and rashes in allergy. When set off, they dump stored chemicals that stir swelling and itch. Small cell bits called polyamines shape much of what cells do. The team found that mast cells carry antizyme inhibitor 2.

They also tested polyamines as fine-tuned dials of one mast cell output: serotonin. A dial that turns one output but not the rest is a rare find. It hints that allergy could be calmed with a light touch. The work ties polyamine control to a cell at the heart of allergy.
plos-pone-0006958:
Britta Björkholm, Chek Mei Bok, Annelie Lundin, and colleagues linked gut microbes to liver function in PLOS ONE in 2009. The liver is the body's central site for breaking down foreign chemicals. Nuclear receptors named CAR and PXR steer much of that drug metabolism. The team asked whether gut bacteria influence this system.

They compared liver gene expression in animals with and without gut microbiota. The microbes changed liver genes and altered chemical metabolism. In other words, gut bacteria help set how the liver handles drugs. That effect may partly explain why drug responses differ between individuals.
plos-pone-0007058:
Paolo Fardin, Marzia Ognibene, Cristina Vanni, and colleagues studied an oncogene in mouse eyes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Dbl protein family is a large group of growth-related proto-oncogenes. Their many parts let them merge signals in networks run by Rho proteins. The team used transgenic mice carrying the Dbl oncogene.

In the lenses of these mice, two changes appeared. Cells underwent an epithelial to mesenchymal transition, loosening their normal form. New vessel growth, called vasculogenesis, also began. Seeing an oncogene reshape the lens shows its reach. It may reveal early steps that tumors borrow later.
plos-pone-0007158: Heiko Stahl, Tanja Fauti, Nina Ullrich, and others studied a small RNA in PLOS ONE in 2009. Blocking that RNA, called miR-155, made helper T cells easier to control. The control came from regulatory T cells, the brakes of the immune system. The cells made easier to rein in were CD4 Th cells. That link is of note for diseases where immune attacks need calming.
plos-pone-0007258:
Patrice Dubreuil, Sébastien Letard, Marco Ciufolini, and colleagues characterized a targeted cancer drug in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The drug is masitinib, also called AB1010. It blocks tyrosine kinases, enzymes that act as growth switches, and it targets the receptor KIT in particular.

KIT is a target in cancer, mastocytosis, and inflammatory diseases. The authors profile masitinib in lab tests and in living animals. They describe it as potent and selective for its targets. Their detailed characterization supported later clinical testing of masitinib in patients with KIT-driven disease worldwide.
plos-pone-0007358:
Mukesh Pasupuleti, Markus Roupe, Victoria Rydengård, and colleagues found an antimicrobial role for the prion protein in 2009. The cellular prion protein sits on cell surfaces throughout the human body. It has many functions, and its exposed front region carries positive charge and binds heparin, features shared by many antimicrobial peptides.

That resemblance prompted the authors to test antimicrobial activity. They report the human prion protein acts against microbes. The activity is mediated by its N-terminal region. Their finding adds a possible defense role to a protein better known for prion diseases.
openalex-w1896237858: Myostatin puts the brakes on muscle growth — knocking it out builds bigger sheep. Crispo and colleagues' 2015 PLoS ONE study efficiently generated myostatin knock-out sheep using CRISPR/Cas9 and microinjection into zygotes. The work brought precise gene editing to farm animals.
openalex-w2111179758: Eradicating malaria needs a research battle plan. A 2011 paper set a research agenda to back malaria elimination. The agenda charted the science needed to stop transmission worldwide — the goal, mapped in full detail for teams.
openalex-w2138134458: A melanoma drug's benefit may track tumor mutations. A 2011 trial asked whether tumor mutation load predicts the drug response in melanoma. The trial tested it as a benefit marker — precision's promise, tested at last for patients now — who benefits most?
openalex-w2154761658: Deworming drugs need benchmark cure rates. A 2011 study tested albendazole's power in schoolchildren. The work set solid egg-count reduction benchmarks for roundworm, whipworm, and hookworm — deworming's yardstick, set at last for programs now.
plos-pone-0006358:
A fixed-dose malaria drug pair, dihydroartemisinin with piperaquine, is a promising drug pair built on artemisinin. Julien Zwang and colleagues pooled individual patient data from seven published studies in a 2009 PLOS ONE analysis. They examined efficacy and tolerability in acute uncomplicated falciparum malaria across multiple centres.

Pooling patient-level data gives a sharper verdict than separate trial summaries. Safety and cure rates can be compared across regions and patient groups. Artemisinin combinations are the backbone of malaria treatment worldwide. Rigorous checks like this guide which combinations health systems should buy. Pooled data of this kind is the best check we have on drugs used by so many.
openalex-w2171372458: Some red blood cells are born different — Southeast Asian ovalocytosis, caused by a small deletion in the band 3 gene, was already known to guard against the deadliest malaria. This 2012 PLoS Medicine study asks whether it also protects children in Papua New Guinea against Plasmodium vivax, the other major malaria parasite. Using two cohorts and a case-control design, the researchers test whether this genetic quirk shields against vivax too.
openalex-w2411750058: Mercury pollution circles the globe, but tracking it takes a global watch. This 2016 Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics paper reports long-term mercury measurements from ground-based sites in the GMOS network — the Global Mercury Observation System. The data map mercury's emission, transport, chemistry, and deposition, vital for understanding how this toxic metal moves through the environment.
openalex-w2588228158: What really drives obesity — too much food, too little movement, or something subtler? In December 2015, the International Agency for Research on Cancer convened experts to review the evidence linking energy balance to obesity. This 2017 paper reports their conclusions on the main drivers, separating what the science supports from what it doesn't.
openalex-w2607179358: Kidney disease is a silent global epidemic — under-recognized, under-treated, and unevenly studied. This 2017 Lancet commission, led by Adeera Levin and colleagues, lays out a roadmap for closing gaps in kidney care, research, and policy worldwide. The report charts where kidney health stands and what must change to protect millions of patients.
openalex-w2803280558: Appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency — and getting the diagnosis right avoids unnecessary operations. This 2018 World Journal of Emergency Surgery paper reports POSAW, a prospective observational study of acute appendicitis around the world. The global snapshot reveals how diagnosis and management vary — and where they can improve.
openalex-w2804562858: Antimicrobial peptides can kill even multiresistant bacteria — but toxicity has blocked their path to the clinic. This 2018 Frontiers in Chemistry paper studies how these peptides interact with model and biological membranes, and how they synergize with conventional antibiotics. The findings guide the design of peptide drugs that kill bacteria without harming patients.
openalex-w2886207958: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor keeps neurons alive, plastic, and communicating — and its disruption marks many brain disorders. This 2018 Molecular Neurobiology paper focuses on BDNF's relationship with neuroinflammation. The review examines how inflammation and this key neurotrophin interact in the diseased brain.
openalex-w2898783558: Sweetpotato feeds millions, especially in sub-Saharan Africa — yet its breeding lags for lack of genomic resources. This 2018 Nature Communications paper sequences two diploid wild relatives of cultivated sweetpotato, revealing targets for genetic improvement. The genomes give breeders the tools to improve a staple that matters most where hunger bites deepest.
openalex-w2917335258: Since the 1990s, the IUIS expert committee has published a biennial classification of inborn errors of immunity. This 2017 Journal of Clinical Immunology paper presents the phenotypic classification for primary immunodeficiencies — a complete catalog and reference for diagnosing these rare immune disorders.
openalex-w2969767558: A decade ago, ocean observing was fragmented — open ocean versus coast, science versus operations. This 2019 Frontiers in Marine Science paper distills what the Framework for Ocean Observing taught the Global Ocean Observing System. The lessons chart how the world learned to watch the seas as one system.
openalex-w2990643258: Basidiomycota — the phylum of mushrooms, rusts, and smuts — is second only to Ascomycota in species numbers. This 2019 Fungal Diversity paper overviews every validly published basidiomycete genus in one document, with divergence times. The single-volume outline is a landmark reference for mycology.
europmc-pmc2807458: The diabetes drug metformin does more than lower blood sugar in this 2010 worm study. Researchers show it puts C. elegans into a state resembling dietary restriction and extends healthy lifespan through the AMPK, LKB1, and SKN-1 pathways. The work maps the molecular chain from drug to longer healthspan. It fueled interest in metformin as a possible anti-aging intervention.
europmc-pmc2821358: Most bladder cancers stay shallow, but some turn invasive, and telling them apart early saves lives. This 2010 paper tests whether a gene classifier can predict progression in primary non-muscle invasive bladder cancer. The authors validate the signature's predictive value. A working test could steer high-risk patients toward aggressive treatment sooner.
europmc-pmc2825658: Toxic byproducts of cells play a two-faced role in ills. This 2010 review looks at how these reactive bits push type 2 diabetes and clogged arteries ahead. The authors trace harm from bits to blood tubes. The take backs care with antioxidants while saying why quick fixes fell flat.
europmc-pmc2833258: Two tiny RNAs act as brakes on bladder cancer in this 2010 study. The authors show miR-145 and miR-133a function as tumor suppressors by directly dialing down FSCN1, a protein that helps cancer cells move. Restoring the microRNAs slowed the cancer. The work identified new molecular handles for bladder cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc2872358: Zinc is a toxin in excess and a must in small doses. This 2010 review weighs zinc's impact on human health, the essential toxin. The authors survey where it helps and harms. Their balancing act guides safe use of a double-edged nutrient.
europmc-pmc2933358: A new drug-resistance gene spread across India, Pakistan, and the UK. This 2010 paper reports the rise of NDM-1, tracing it with lab, clinical, and field data. The authors' alarm rang worldwide. Their work spurred the global fight against superbugs.
europmc-pmc2958458: Malignant belly fluid met a three-armed antibody in this 2010 trial. The authors test catumaxomab for malignant ascites from epithelial cancer in a randomized phase II/III trial. Their result backed the drug. The trial advanced a novel therapy. It was among the first trifunctional antibodies tested.
europmc-pmc2996858: Pig gum disease met stem cell therapy. This 2010 paper tests donor gum-ligament stem cells against gum disease in pigs. The authors' trial shows real healing. Their work points to tooth-saving treatments. Human trials followed the pig success. Regrown ligaments may anchor loose teeth.
europmc-pmc3000358: HIV's shell is a druggable target. This 2010 paper argues the virus's protein shell can be hit with small-molecule drugs. The authors lay out the case. Their work opened a new drug front. Capsid blockers later reached the clinic. Lenacapavir traces its roots to this pitch.
europmc-pmc3017758: Family trees need clean DNA lineups. This 2010 paper brings BMGE, software that picks the most telling parts of DNA lineups. The authors' tool trims noisy columns. Their software spread through labs. Tree builders run it before every analysis. Cleaner inputs yield truer family trees.
europmc-pmc3061958: Focus groups rarely report their size well. This 2011 paper audits how focus-group studies report their headcounts. The authors find sloppy habits. Their work pushed better standards. Many papers omit the number entirely. Journals now ask for the headcount. The audit covered hundreds of studies.
europmc-pmc3108958: Preemies' gut germs shift before bowel disaster. This 2011 paper studies fecal microbiota in premature infants before necrotizing enterocolitis strikes. The authors spot warning shifts. Their work points to early screening. Proteobacteria bloomed before illness hit. NICUs now watch stool samples closely.
europmc-pmc3111658: Talk therapy access got a UK test. This 2009 paper evaluates two demonstration sites for wider psychological therapy. The authors report early wins. Their work launched a national program. Thousands got help sooner, they found. The model spread across England. Recovery rates matched clinical trials.
europmc-pmc3197658: Random gene signatures fooled cancer prediction. This 2011 paper shows most random gene signatures link to breast cancer outcome. The authors expose the artifact. Their work humbled the field. Proliferation genes drove the illusion. Signature papers now face tougher review. The paper is a cautionary classic.
europmc-pmc3252258: Stressed plants got a systems view. This 2011 paper reviews how plants handle drought, salt, and heat as whole systems. The authors map the networks. Their overview guides breeding. Shared stress hubs emerged, they found. Breeders target the hub genes. The review is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3280258: Depression's heart risk got measured. This 2012 paper links depression and anxiety to blunted heart-rate variability. The authors reveal the risk. Their work guides care. Anxiety compounded the effect. Cardiologists took note, they say. Kemp's team led the work. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3314658: RSV got a new genotype. This 2012 paper finds a novel RSV strain in Ontario with a duplicated gene. The authors reveal the duplication. Their work guides surveillance. The strain spread fast, they found. Eshaghi's team led the work. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3320358: Pig farmers' staph got compared. This 2005 paper compares staph strains from pig farmers, controls, and pigs. The authors reveal the shared clones. Their work guides hygiene. Farmers carried pig strains. Armand-Lefevre's team led the work. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3374458: Hantavirus found an African mouse. This 2006 paper reports a new hantavirus in a Guinean wood mouse. The authors reveal the host. Their work guides surveillance. Klempa's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It expanded the virus map.
